title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
會試錄序
皇上嗣大歷服九年于兹矣凡内
脩外攘究圖于
淵衷而更張其敝弛以恢弘治
道者鉅細罔間其於科目一
事尤惓惓加之意蓋以科目
寔賢才所從出重科目斯得
===
賢才則於致治也何有廼成
化壬辰春二月適禮部會試
天下貢士之期先日尚書臣
榦侍郎臣吉臣雷復以
聞特詔舉行之如故事仍
命臣安臣朝宗為主考其同考則
侍講臣教脩撰臣健臣璟臣

皇上嗣大歷服，九年于兹矣。凡内脩外攘，究圖于淵衷，而更張其敝弛，以恢弘治道者，鉅細罔間。其於科目一事，尤惓惓加之意。蓋以科目寔賢才所從出，重科目斯得賢才，則於致治也何有？廼成化壬辰春二月，適禮部會試天下貢士之期。先日，尚書臣榦、侍郎臣吉、臣雷復以聞，特詔舉行之如故事。仍命臣安、臣朝宗為主考；其同考則侍講臣教，脩撰臣健、臣璟、臣
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

It is now nine years since His Majesty succeeded to the great dynastic mandate and governance. In all matters of domestic cultivation and foreign defense, He has thoroughly deliberated within His profound mind and reformed what was corrupt or lax in order to expand and magnify the way of governance, overlooking nothing whether great or small. Toward the matter of the civil service examinations in particular, He has devoted earnest and unceasing attention. This is because the civil service examinations are truly the source from which worthy talents emerge; if the examinations are valued, worthy talents will be obtained, and what difficulty will there then be in achieving good governance? Now, in the second month of spring of the renchen year of the Chenghua era [1472], the time arrived for the Ministry of Rites to conduct the Metropolitan Examination for the tribute scholars of the Empire. On a preceding day, Your Majesty's servants Minister [Zou] Gan, and Vice Ministers [Yin] Ji and [Ye] Sheng reported this to the Throne, and a special imperial decree ordered that it be carried out according to precedent. Furthermore, Your Majesty commanded Your servants [Wan] An and [Jiang] Chaozong to serve as Chief Examiners; as for the Associate Examiners, they were Expositor-in-Waiting Your servant [Peng] Jiao, Senior Compilers Your servants [Liu] Jian, [Chen] Jing, and Your servant…

title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
昇編脩臣芳臣登檢討臣顓
臣希賢給事中臣理員外郎臣
孔昭署員外郎臣弘主事臣瑜
監試則御史臣忠臣昉綱維
其事則又臣吉也至日自
陛辭以往臣等暨内外諸執事
咸矢心竭誠各共廼職期以
簡拔賢儁用輔翊我
國家億萬年太平之祚於無疆
自鎖院出題凡三試之乃於
三千四百餘卷中嚴考校公
去取遵
宸斷得二百有五十人焉
也於戲亦盛矣哉仰惟我

translation_en:
… Sheng 昇; Historiographers (Bianxiu) your servants Fang 芳 and Deng 登; Investigating Editors (Jiantao) your servants Zhuan 顓 and Xixian 希賢; Supervising Secretary (Jishizhong) your servant Li 理; Vice Director (Yuanwailang) your servant Kongzhao 孔昭; Acting Vice Director (Shu Yuanwailang) your servant Hong 弘; and Secretary (Zhushi) your servant Yu 瑜. Serving as Examination Supervisors (Jianshi) were Investigating Censors (Yushi) your servants Zhong 忠 and Fang 昉, while the one who directed and coordinated the affairs as a whole was again your servant Ji 吉.

When the day arrived, from the moment we took leave of the throne and proceeded to our posts, your servants together with all the inner and outer functionaries vowed in our hearts to exhaust our sincerity, each reverently fulfilling his duties, hoping to select worthy and eminent talents to assist and uphold our Dynasty's boundless fortune of peace for hundreds of millions of years. Once the examination compound was locked and the questions were issued, the candidates were tested in three sessions. Then, from among more than 3,400 examination papers, we conducted a rigorous evaluation and made impartial selections and rejections, and in compliance with the Imperial decision we obtained 250 men.

title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
國家
祖宗聖德上格
天心天為生賢以資佐理
聖化又從而造就之出而任使咸
著勳名故其得人之盛治效
之隆真誠追配隆古迄我
皇上懋昭大德
===
天命之祐相者益加克敦化原海
隅之冒蒙者愈至肆今多士
為天所生為
上所化者顒顒而起胥於科目焉
出夫豈偶然之故哉且天之
生我而賦予之者莫大夫仁
義禮智

皇上懋昭大德
天命之祜相者益加克敦化原海
隅之冐蒙者愈至肆今多士
為天所生為
===
上所化者顯顯而起晉於科目焉
出夫豈偶然之故哉且天之
生我而賦予之者莫大夫仁
義禮智
punctuated: 國家祖宗聖德，上格天心，天為生賢以資佐理，聖化又從而造就之，出而任使，咸著勳名。故其得人之盛，治效之隆，真誠追配隆古。迄我皇上，懋昭大德，天命之祐相者益加，克敦化原，海隅之冒蒙者愈至。肆今多士，為天所生，為上所化者，顒顒而起，胥於科目焉出，夫豈偶然之故哉！且天之生我而賦予之者，莫大夫仁義禮智；
translation_en: … Dynastic State, the sacred virtue of the Imperial Ancestors reached up to the mind of Heaven. Heaven therefore brought forth worthy talents to assist in governance, and the sacred transformative influence in turn nurtured and molded them; when they went forth to be employed in office, they all achieved meritorious renown. Thus, the abundance of talented men obtained and the splendor of the results of governance truly rivaled those of high antiquity. Down to Our Emperor, who exerts himself to manifest great virtue, the blessings and aid of the Mandate of Heaven have increased ever more; able to enrich the source of transformation, those in the farthest corners of the seas who are covered by his grace are ever more thoroughly reached. Therefore, today the multitude of scholars—brought forth by Heaven and transformed by the Sovereign—rise up in reverent aspiration and all emerge through the examination system. How could this be by mere chance? Moreover, in Heaven's giving birth to us and endowing us with our nature, nothing is greater than benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom; …

title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
上之化我而造就之者不越夫詩
書禮樂詩書禮樂即所以明
仁義禮智者也諸士於此蘊
蓄於心既發為文章膺薦而
来得預茲選行將以之奉對
清問策名科第其拜官受直可
指日俟矣何可舍此而不之
===
務邪尚仁以宅心義以質事
禮節夫此智別夫此俾內焉
事
君股肱耳目之足託而
社稷賴以安外焉臨民藩垣屏翰
之足寄而黎庶遂其願夫然
庶足以彰我

translation_en: … and that by which the Sovereign transforms us and brings us to accomplishment goes no further than the Odes, the Documents, Rites, and Music. The Odes, the Documents, Rites, and Music are precisely the means to illuminate benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom. Having treasured these in their hearts and expressed them in literary compositions, the scholars have received recommendations to come here and participate in this selection. Soon they will employ them to respond to the Emperor's pure inquiries and have their names inscribed on the examination rolls; their appointment to office and receipt of emoluments may be awaited within days. How could they cast these aside and not devote themselves to them? Let them esteem benevolence as the dwelling of the mind, and righteousness as the substance of affairs, regulating these with propriety and discriminating them with wisdom. Thus, when serving the Sovereign within the court, they will be worthy of being entrusted as his limbs, ears, and eyes, so that the altars of state may rely on them for peace; when governing the people in the provinces, they will be worthy of being charged as bulwarks and shields, so that the common multitude may fulfill their desires. title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
皇上得人之盛治效之隆蓋與
祖宗之世前後猶一日也借曰煦
煦其仁大體或未務孑孑其
義大節或未保瑣瑣其禮大
本或未恤察察其智大指或
未達則職業臧否可知已其
於
===
天之生我與
上之化我兩爲有負而於科目寧
不有玷歟事既竣例有錄
進呈僉以為宜序引諸端也故
不辭謹書此與諸士勉圖之
通議大夫禮部左侍郎兼翰
林院學士萬安謹序

天之生我與
上之化我兩爲有負而於科目寧
不有玷歟事既竣例有錄
進呈僉以爲宜序引諸端也故
不辭謹書以與諸士勉圖之
通議大夫禮部左侍郎兼翰
林院學士萬安謹序
punctuated:
皇上得人之盛、治效之隆，蓋與祖宗之世前後猶一日也。借曰煦煦其仁，大體或未務；孑孑其義，大節或未保；瑣瑣其禮，大本或未恤；察察其智，大指或未達；則職業臧否可知已。其於天之生我與上之化我，兩爲有負，而於科目寧不有玷歟？事既竣，例有錄進呈，僉以為宜序引諸端也。故不辭，謹書此與諸士勉圖之。
通議大夫、禮部左侍郎兼翰林院學士萬安謹序。
translation_en:
…the abundance of capable men obtained by His Majesty and the flourishing results of his governance will indeed be as one with the eras of the Imperial Ancestors, past and present alike. Suppose instead that one practices a petty benevolence while perhaps neglecting the grand framework; clings to an isolated righteousness while perhaps failing to preserve great integrity; busies oneself with trivial rites while perhaps disregarding the fundamental basis; or prides oneself on a nitpicking wisdom while perhaps failing to grasp the overarching aim—then the success or failure of one's official duties is already clear enough. Would this not fail both Heaven that gave us life and the Sovereign who transformed us, and how could it not bring blemish to the examination system? Now that the affair is concluded, by precedent a record is to be presented to the throne, and all deemed it fitting that I write a preface to introduce its beginning. Therefore I have not declined, and respectfully write these words to encourage the scholars in their endeavors.
Respectfully prefaced by Wan An 萬安, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel, Left Vice Minister of Rites, concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy.

translation_en:
Metropolitan Examination of the Eighth Year of the Chenghua Reign (1472)

Administrators of the Memorialized Examinations
Zou Gan 鄒榦, Grand Master for Assisting toward Good Governance and Minister of Rites (courtesy name Zongsheng 宗盛, a native of Yuhang County, Zhejiang, and a metropolitan graduate of the jiwei year [1439]).

title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
第壹塲
四書
百工居肆以成其事君子學以致其道
夫孝者善繼人之志善述人之事者也春
秋脩其祖廟陳其宗器設其裳衣薦
其時食宗廟之禮所以序昭穆也序
爵所以辨貴賤也序事所以辨賢也
旅酬下為上所以逮賤也燕毛所以
序齒也踐其位行其禮奏其樂敬其
===
所尊愛其所親
文王以民力為臺為沼而民歡樂之謂其
臺曰靈臺謂其沼曰靈沼樂其有麋
鹿魚鼈古之人與民偕樂故能樂也
易
至靜而德方
日月得天而能久照四時變化而能久成
聖人久於其道而天下化成
一陰一陽之謂道繼之者善也成之者性

First Session

The Four Books

"The artisans dwell in their workshops in order to accomplish their work; the superior man learns in order to reach the utmost of his Way."

"Now filial piety is the skillful carrying on of the wishes of our forefathers, and the skillful carrying forward of their undertakings. In spring and autumn, they repaired and beautified the temple-halls of their fathers, set forth their ancestral vessels, displayed their various robes, and presented the offerings of the several seasons. By means of the ceremonies of the ancestral temple, they distinguished the royal kindred according to their order of descent. By ordering the ranks of nobility, they distinguished the more noble and the less. By the arrangement of the services, they made a distinction of talents and worth. In the ceremony of general pledging, the inferiors presented the cup to their superiors, and thus something was given the lowest to do. At the concluding feast, places were given according to the hair, and thus was made the distinction of years. They occupied the places of their forefathers, practiced their ceremonies, and performed their music. They reverenced those whom they honored, and loved those whom they held dear."

"King Wen used the strength of the people to make his tower and his pond, and yet the people rejoiced to do the work, calling the tower 'The Marvelous Tower,' and the pond 'The Marvelous Pond,' rejoicing that he had his large deer, his fishes, and his turtles. The ancients shared their pleasures with the people, and therefore they were able to enjoy them."

Book of Changes (Yijing)

"Wait in supreme stillness, and its virtue is square."

"The sun and moon have their place in heaven, and are able to shine forever. The four seasons change and transform, and are able to bring things to maturity forever. The sage continues long in his Way, and all under heaven are transformed and brought to completion."

"One yin and one yang—this is called the Way. That which ensues from it is goodness; that which brings it to completion is the nature…"

Chao Wu of Cai fled to Zheng; [15th year of Duke Zhao] Marquis Zhu of Cai fled to Chu; [21st year of Duke Zhao] Wu entered Ying. [4th year of Duke Ding]

Record of Rites (Liji):
"Therefore, man is the virtue of Heaven and Earth, the interaction of yin and yang, the convergence of ghosts and spirits, and the finest essence of the Five Phases."
"'What you have said is indeed great, admirable, and magnificent! Does the discussion end with this and nothing more?' Confucius said, 'How could that be so! When the noble man practices them, there are still five further developments in their application.'"
"When the sages established rules of conduct, they did not frame them on the basis of themselves alone; they caused the people to have that by which they felt encouraged to strive and ashamed of failing, so as to carry out their words. Ritual was used to regulate them, trustworthiness to bind them, deportment to refine them, clothing to transform them, and friends to bring them to the utmost standard, desiring that the people should possess uniformity of purpose."
"Therefore, the noble man hears much, verifies it, and holds fast to it; remembers much, verifies it, and keeps it close; discerns with precision, selects the essentials, and puts them into practice."

title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
養其身保全其命則君也是人道大端
莫有先於敬天忠君孝親三事者伊欲
盡兹三事以無媿乎為人之道其要安
在六經孔子所刪述具載古人克盡斯
道者多矣其大而可法者可槩指歟孔
門舉此問荅者非一矣其切而易行者
可槩陳歟洪惟我
聖朝
太祖高皇帝萬幾之暇條成
===
大誥三編無非所以扶持世道也其於六經
孔門之言有合歟間有闡明斯道者可
厯指歟嘗
致齋便殿有感
淵衷爰命儒臣纂輯精誠錄一書無非所以
發明斯道也果皆六經孔門之言歟間
有取於他書者可厯數歟竊嘗誦讀而
疑之祀天天子事也臣下不敢僭豈天
在人臣有弗當敬歟忠君人臣事也君

translation_en:
…sustaining one's body and preserving one's life comes from the ruler. Thus, among the great fundamentals of the human way, none takes precedence over these three matters: revering Heaven, being loyal to the ruler, and being filial to one's parents. If one wishes to fulfill these three matters completely so as not to feel ashamed before the way of being human, wherein lies the essential key? The Six Classics, edited and transmitted by Confucius, record in full many ancients who were able to fulfill this Way; can the greatest and most worthy of emulation among them be generally pointed out? The questions and answers raised on these matters within the school of Confucius were not few; can those that are most pertinent and easy to practice be generally set forth?

Reflecting upon our sacred dynasty, Emperor Taizu Gaohuangdi, in his leisure from the myriad affairs of state, compiled in articles the three parts of the Grand Pronouncements (Dagao), all of which were meant to uphold the moral order of the world. Do they accord with the words of the Six Classics and the school of Confucius? Where they occasionally elucidate this Way, can those passages be pointed out one by one? Once, while observing abstinence in a side palace and feeling moved in the depths of his heart, he thereupon commanded Confucian officials to compile the book Record of Utmost Sincerity (Jingcheng lu), which likewise was entirely meant to illuminate this Way. Does it indeed consist solely of the words of the Six Classics and the school of Confucius? Where it occasionally draws from other books, can those sources be enumerated one by one?

I have privately recited and read these and had doubts about them: sacrificing to Heaven is the business of the Son of Heaven, which subjects below dare not usurp—could it be that for a subject, Heaven ought not to be revered? Being loyal to the ruler is the business of a subject, whereas the ruler…

title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
上若無所與豈人君果無所事於忠歟
之斯三者皆上下之所通行而行之貴
得其要苟得其要則道無往而不盡效
亦無往而不著也夫弊弊於往籍而於
當代之訓漫弗之究汲汲於外務而於切己
之事或未之遑君子所不取諸士固不
如是也宜詳悉以對
問子朱子謂論語孟子大學中庸四書為
學問之根本其發明訓釋可謂無餘蘊
===
矣試舉其所論者相與講之論語孟子
秦漢諸儒類能言之其去古未遠宜有
得矣而不為朱子所取者其失何在大
學中庸韓子蘇子亦嘗言之彼皆文章
魁傑宜有當矣而為朱子所少者其說
何指謂論語之要在於操存涵養其所
以為操存為涵養者當何如其為功孟
子之要在於體驗擴充其所以為體驗
為擴充者當何如其致力大學首言明

punctuated:
上若無所與，豈人君果無所事於忠歟？之斯三者，皆上下之所通行，而行之貴得其要。苟得其要，則道無往而不盡，效亦無往而不著也。夫弊弊於往籍，而於當代之訓漫弗之究；汲汲於外務，而於切己之事或未之遑，君子所不取。諸士固不如是也，宜詳悉以對。

問：子朱子謂《論語》、《孟子》、《大學》、《中庸》四書為學問之根本，其發明訓釋，可謂無餘蘊矣。試舉其所論者相與講之。《論語》、《孟子》，秦、漢諸儒類能言之，其去古未遠，宜有得矣，而不為朱子所取者，其失何在？《大學》、《中庸》，韓子、蘇子亦嘗言之，彼皆文章魁傑，宜有當矣，而為朱子所少者，其說何指？謂《論語》之要在於操存涵養，其所以為操存、為涵養者，當何如其為功？《孟子》之要在於體驗擴充，其所以為體驗、為擴充者，當何如其致力？《大學》首言明…
translation_en:
…the sovereign above seems to have no part in it, yet does a ruler truly have no business with loyalty? These three matters are all practiced alike by those above and below, and in practicing them, the important thing is to grasp their essentials. If one grasps their essentials, then the Way will be fulfilled everywhere, and its efficacy will likewise be manifest everywhere. Now, to toil exhaustively over ancient texts while negligently failing to examine the instructions of the reigning dynasty, or to busy oneself anxiously with external affairs while having no leisure for matters of immediate personal concern—this the gentleman does not approve. You scholars are surely not like this; you should reply in full detail.

Question: Master Zhu [Zhu Xi 朱熹] said that the Four Books—the Analects (Lunyu), the Mencius (Mengzi), the Great Learning (Daxue), and the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong)—are the foundation of learning, and his elucidation and exegesis of them may be said to have left nothing unexhausted. Let us cite what he discussed and examine it together. As for the Analects and the Mencius, the various Confucian scholars of the Qin and Han dynasties were generally able to speak of them. Since they were not far removed from antiquity, they ought to have grasped something of them; yet they were not accepted by Master Zhu—wherein lay their failure? As for the Great Learning and the Doctrine of the Mean, Master Han [Han Yu 韓愈] and Master Su [Su Shi 蘇軾 or Su Zhe 蘇轍] also once spoke of them. They were both towering figures in literature and ought to have hit the mark; yet they were disparaged by Master Zhu—to what did their doctrines point? It is said that the essential point of the Analects lies in preserving and nurturing [the mind]; by what sort of effort does one carry out this preserving and this nurturing? The essential point of the Mencius lies in personal realization and extension [of innate goodness]; by what sort of exertion does one carry out this personal realization and this extension? The Great Learning begins by speaking of manifesting…

title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
德新民為一書之綱領未嘗言敬何以
又謂始終不外乎敬中庸首言性道教
為一篇之體要未嘗語誠何以又謂樞
紐不外夫誠大學為入德之門程子之
言也而或者又謂六經門戸自中庸入
觀聖人之道當自孟子始此韓子之言
也而程子又謂孟子才高無據當學顏
子是皆朱子之所取者何不同歟大學
格物致知之傳既補矣而或者謂其錯
===
簡在經文中中庸尊德性道問學之註
亦精矣而諸儒於存心致知紛紜其論
是皆朱子之所定者果有遺歟諸生習
誦有年考其異而會其同必有至當之
論詳著于篇以觀所學
問人才致治之具古之為天下者未嘗不
重之以成治而為士者亦未嘗不自重
以待用世降風移固有朝扣秦關暮游
燕璧以求售者而人之所以重之與士

重之以成治而爲士者亦未嘗不自重
以待用世降風移固有朝扣秦關莫游
燕壁以求售者而人之所以重之與士
punctuated:
德、新民為一書之綱領，未嘗言敬，何以又謂始終不外乎敬？《中庸》首言性、道、教為一篇之體要，未嘗語誠，何以又謂樞紐不外夫誠？「《大學》為入德之門」，程子之言也；而或者又謂「《六經》門戸自《中庸》入」。「觀聖人之道當自《孟子》始」，此韓子之言也；而程子又謂「孟子才高無據，當學顏子」。是皆朱子之所取者，何不同歟？《大學》格物致知之傳既補矣，而或者謂其錯簡在經文中；《中庸》尊德性、道問學之註亦精矣，而諸儒於存心、致知紛紜其論。是皆朱子之所定者，果有遺歟？諸生習誦有年，考其異而會其同，必有至當之論，詳著于篇，以觀所學。
問：人才，致治之具。古之為天下者，未嘗不重之以成治；而為士者，亦未嘗不自重以待用。世降風移，固有朝扣秦關、暮游燕璧以求售者，而人之所以重之與士…
translation_en:
…“manifesting luminous virtue” and “renewing the people” as the guiding principles of the entire book, without ever mentioning “reverence” (jing 敬); why then is it also said that from beginning to end it goes no further than reverence? The Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong 中庸) begins by speaking of “nature,” “the Way,” and “instruction” as the essential substance of the entire work, without ever speaking of “sincerity” (cheng 誠); why then is it also said that its pivot goes no further than sincerity? That “the Great Learning (Daxue 大學) is the gate through which one enters virtue” is the statement of Master Cheng 程子; yet some say instead that “the gateway to the Six Classics is entered through the Doctrine of the Mean.” “To observe the Way of the Sages, one should begin with the Mencius (Mengzi 孟子)”—this is the statement of Master Han 韓子 [Han Yu 韓愈]; yet Master Cheng also said, “Mencius’s talent was lofty and leaves nothing to take hold of; one should instead learn from Master Yan 顏子 [Yan Hui 顏回].” All of these were endorsed by Master Zhu 朱子 [Zhu Xi 朱熹]—why do they differ? In the Great Learning, the commentary chapter on “investigating things and extending knowledge” was already supplemented [by Zhu Xi], yet some claim that the misplaced slips are actually still within the Classic text itself. In the Doctrine of the Mean, the commentary on “honoring the moral nature and following the path of inquiry and study” is likewise precise, yet various scholars have engaged in confused and divergent debates over “preserving the mind” and “extending knowledge.” All of these were settled by Master Zhu—did he indeed leave something out? You students have recited and studied these texts for years; having examined their differences and synthesized their commonalities, you must certainly hold the most fitting conclusions. Set them forth in detail in your essays, so that we may observe what you have learned.

Question: Men of talent are the instruments for bringing about good governance. Those in antiquity who governed the Empire never failed to value them in order to achieve order, and those who were scholars likewise never failed to value themselves while awaiting employment. As the ages declined and customs shifted, there were indeed those who knocked at the passes of Qin 秦 in the morning and traveled to the jade-courts [?] of Yan 燕 in the evening in order to hawk their skills, and thus the way in which rulers valued them and the way in which scholars…

title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
之所以自重者衰矣今
聖明在上用人如不及才而未用者網之於科
目用而克稱者歷試而益崇其所以重
之者至矣而士未盡能自重其故何歟
將欲設為隄防以禁之歟恐奔潰四出
又有不可遏者將欲聽其自尔而不之
禁歟恐人心日趨莫之止極其患有不
可勝言者或以為舜命九官終身不易
周分六職不聞數遷法制素明人志素
===
定則所謂奔競者不待禁而自無也或
以為禁之於彼不若開之於此與其杜
奔競不若獎恬退使恬退者得進而奔
競者無効則人又將趨其所不趨矣或
又以為爵祿者人主所以奔走天下之
術也誠使天下之士皆無求於世人主
誰與理天下噫三者之說不一也欲救
今日之弊果法制所當先歟抑激勸有
不容已者歟抑別有其說歟願為我言

今日之弊彙法制所當先歟抑激勸有
不容已者歟抑別有其說歟願熹哉言
punctuated: 之所以自重者衰矣。今聖明在上，用人如不及：才而未用者，網之於科目；用而克稱者，歷試而益崇。其所以重之者至矣，而士未盡能自重，其故何歟？將欲設為隄防以禁之歟？恐奔潰四出，又有不可遏者。將欲聽其自尔而不之禁歟？恐人心日趨，莫之止極，其患有不可勝言者。或以為舜命九官，終身不易；周分六職，不聞數遷。法制素明，人志素定，則所謂奔競者，不待禁而自無也。或以為禁之於彼，不若開之於此；與其杜奔競，不若獎恬退。使恬退者得進，而奔競者無効，則人又將趨其所不趨矣。或又以為爵祿者，人主所以奔走天下之術也。誠使天下之士皆無求於世，人主誰與理天下？噫！三者之說不一也。欲救今日之弊，果法制所當先歟？抑激勸有不容已者歟？抑別有其說歟？願為我言…
translation_en:
…by which scholars valued themselves declined. Today, the Sacred and Enlightened Emperor is on the throne, and he employs men as if fearing he might fall short: those who have talent but are not yet employed are gathered in through the examination categories; those who are employed and prove equal to their offices are tested through successive posts and ever more exalted. The ways in which he values them have reached the utmost, and yet scholars are not all able to value themselves—what is the reason for this? Should we set up dikes and barriers to prohibit such behavior? One fears that they would burst forth in all directions and prove impossible to check. Or should we leave them as they are and not prohibit them? One fears that men's minds would daily rush onward without limit, and the resulting harms would be beyond description.

Some hold that Shun appointed the Nine Officers and did not change them for life, and that the Zhou divided the Six Offices and were not heard to make frequent transfers. When institutional regulations are long clear and men's ambitions long settled, then what is called scrambling for advancement disappears of itself without waiting to be prohibited. Others hold that prohibiting them on that side is not as good as opening a path on this side, and that rather than blocking scrambling for advancement, it is better to reward quiet modesty and retirement. If the modest and retiring are enabled to advance while the scrambling gain no results, then men will in turn rush toward that which they previously did not pursue! Yet others hold that ranks and emoluments are the art by which the ruler sets the world in motion. If indeed all the scholars of the world sought nothing from the age, with whom would the ruler govern the world?

Alas! The arguments of these three sides are not uniform. In seeking to remedy the abuses of the present day, is it indeed institutional regulations that should come first? Or is encouragement through reward and admonition something that cannot be dispensed with? Or is there yet another explanation? I wish you to state it for me…

問：兵戎，國之大事，學者所宜知也。今朝廷用師西陲，其強弱、利害、長短、得失之故，有可得而論者。在六國時，秦僅有今關中之地，而齊、楚、韓、魏、燕、趙又與為敵國；然而當是時也，攘却西戎至千餘里。今也天下為一，外兼秦、晉之勢，內引百郡為助，強壯盛大，固非當日擬矣。宋之中葉，嘗有西事；然是時也，疆場之限近在鄜、延，山川之險與敵共之，蓋亦無恠乎其難為功也。今也北跨大河之曲，西盡涼、夏之地，娭勢利便，又非異時比矣。中國之技，昔人所謂夷狄十不足以當四五者也；今魚麗而守，蟻聚而戰，又未嘗不倍十其數矣。敵加於己，不得已而起，昔人所謂應兵而勝者也；今釁不自我，端每由之，迫而後動，又非得已不已之舉矣。夫以區區小虜，而理勢之論，今昔…
translation_en:
…it.

Question: Military affairs are a great matter of state, something that scholars ought to understand. At present, the imperial court is deploying troops on the western frontier, and the reasons behind the relative strength and weakness, advantages and disadvantages, merits and shortcomings, and successes and failures involved are matters that can be discussed. During the era of the Six States, Qin possessed only the territory of present-day Guanzhong, while Qi, Chu, Han, Wei, Yan, and Zhao stood against it as rival states; yet even at that time, it drove back the Western Rong by more than a thousand li. Today, all under Heaven is united as one: externally we combine the strategic positions of Qin and Jin, and internally we draw upon a hundred commanderies for support—our strength, vigor, and grandeur are certainly beyond comparison with those days. In the middle period of the Song dynasty, there were also military campaigns in the west; yet at that time, the frontier boundary lay close by in Fu and Yan, and the strategic passes of mountains and rivers were shared with the enemy, so it is no wonder that it was difficult to achieve success. Today, our territory straddles the bend of the Yellow River in the north and extends to the farthest reaches of Liang and Xia in the west; the advantage and convenience of our strategic topography [?] are likewise incomparable to those of former times. As for the martial skills of the Central States, people of the past said that ten of the Yi and Di barbarians were not enough to match four or five of ours; today, arrayed in fish-scale formations for defense and massed like ants in battle, our numbers have never failed to be double or tenfold theirs. When the enemy attacks us and we rise up only because we have no choice, this is what people of the past called "responding troops," who are bound to triumph; today, the provocations do not originate with us, the incidents are always started by them, and we move only when compelled—so these are by no means campaigns undertaken when they could have been avoided. Now, faced with such petty, insignificant caitiffs, and when the assessment of right and strategic advantage between the present and the past…

punctuated:
之殊又如此，乃厪廟朝之議，以勞西人，其故不可不論也。以戰，必求我之所以勝；以守，必制彼之無以来；以恩，必使其無玩；以威，必使其無抗：何以能然也？昔諸葛孔明策計孫、曹，規取蜀、漢；范仲淹為書區條時務，其於天下事，固已反復熟爛於窮居之日矣。我懷若人，庶其有遇。茲不以廋詞隐義相困，顧因以得孔明、仲淹者薦聞于上，固區區以人事君之誠也。

問：歷代建都，莫不據形勝以臨天下，然而供億未嘗不仰給於漕運也。其開濬、轉運，必得人而後能濟，否則未免有壅滯之患、告匱之憂，考之載籍，盖可見已。彼漢之長安、唐之關洛、宋之大梁，其轉運之迹，可得而言歟？其增廣之漸，可得而陳歟？夫三代之都，皆在雍、豫之間，而或仰於山東，或仰於江淮者，何歟？所任之
translation_en:
… between past and present is also like this; yet it still troubles the deliberations of the court and exhausts the people of the west—the reasons for this cannot go undiscussed. In warfare, how can we be sure to secure the means of our victory? In defense, how can we be sure to prevent them from coming? In showing grace, how can we be sure to keep them from growing insolent? In wielding awe, how can we be sure to keep them from resisting? By what means can this be achieved? In the past, Zhuge Kong明 (Zhuge Liang 諸葛亮) devised strategies regarding Sun [Quan] and Cao [Cao] and planned the capture of Shu and Han; Fan Zhongyan 范仲淹 wrote memorials itemizing current affairs. Regarding the affairs of the empire, they had certainly already turned them over and mastered them thoroughly during their days of living in obscurity. I long for such men, hoping perhaps to encounter them. Here I do not perplex you with riddles or hidden meanings, looking instead to obtain by this means men like Kongming and Zhongyan to recommend to the Emperor—this is truly my humble sincerity in serving the ruler by bringing forward capable men.

Question: In establishing their capitals, successive dynasties have without exception occupied strategic terrain from which to oversee the empire; yet for their provisioning they have never failed to rely upon canal and river grain transport. Its dredging and shipment must obtain the right men before they can succeed; otherwise, one cannot avoid the affliction of blockage and stagnation or the worry of exhaustion of supplies. Examining the historical records, this can indeed be seen. As for Chang'an 長安 in the Han, Guanzhong 關中 and Luoyang 洛陽 in the Tang, and Daliang 大梁 (Kaifeng) in the Song—can the traces of their transport systems be recounted? Can the gradual process of their expansion be set forth? Now, the capitals of the Three Dynasties [herein referring to Han, Tang, and Song] were all located between Yongzhou 雍州 and Yuzhou 豫州; why is it that some relied on Shandong 山東 while others relied on the Jiang-Huai 江淮 region? The men appointed to these tasks …

punctuated: 人，皆一時之選，而或推其足國，或咎其厲民，何歟？聖朝建立兩京，誠有以據天下之形勝，殆非漢、唐、宋之比。南京遠近輻輳，水陸咸便，固無容論。京師自江淮數千餘里，直抵通州，開濬轉運，悉有良規，盖我太宗文皇帝之成畫，而委託之得人也。其經理之制，於古何取？轉運之效，於古何如？惟通州距都城僅一舍餘耳，僦車陸輓，費動鉅萬，每或不給，輒貸以償，歲復一歲，不勝罷困，雖有為國愛民者，莫之如何。近代運河閘壩具存，文皇帝嘗設置防守，欲興復之，未遑也。迩因臣下建白，特詔修濬，盖欲紓今日之急，成萬世之利也。心竊疑之：畿內比歲不登，修之則勞費不貲，或怨讟繁興；不修則江南日困，或
translation_en:
…men [appointed to the task] were all the finest choices of their age; yet why were some praised for enriching the state, while others were blamed for oppressing the people?

Our sacred dynasty has established the Two Capitals, truly occupying the strategic strongholds of the realm in a manner scarcely comparable to that of the Han, Tang, or Song. With the Southern Capital (Nanjing), where routes from near and far converge like spokes at a hub and both water and land transport are convenient, there is assuredly no need for discussion. As for the Capital (Beijing), stretching several thousand li from the Yangtze and Huai regions straight to Tongzhou, the dredging of canals and the relay transport of grain all follow sound regulations. This is indeed due to the established plan of our Emperor Taizong Wen (the Yongle Emperor) and his entrusting the task to the right men. In his system of administration, what did he adopt from antiquity? And how does the effectiveness of his transport system compare with that of antiquity?

Yet Tongzhou is barely more than thirty li (one she) from the capital city. Hiring carts to haul the grain overland costs tens of thousands at a turn. Whenever the funds fall short, loans are immediately taken out to make up the difference; year after year, the people cannot bear the exhaustion and distress, and even though there are those who serve the state and love the people, they can do nothing about it. The locks and dams of the canal from the recent era (the Yuan dynasty) remain intact. Emperor Wen once established guards and defenses there, intending to restore the waterway, but had no leisure to complete it. Recently, in response to proposals submitted by officials, the Emperor issued a special decree to repair and dredge it, wishing thereby to relieve the urgent difficulties of today and secure an advantage for ten thousand generations. Yet in my heart I privately harbor doubts: in the Metropolitan Area, harvests have failed in consecutive years; if we repair it, the labor and expense will be immeasurable, and bitter resentment may arise on all sides; if we do not repair it, Jiangnan (the region south of the Yangtze) will grow more distressed by the day, and…

title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
百工居肆以成其事君子學以致其道
李仁傑
同考試官編修商批能兼二說而措詞簡
當者僅見此篇
同考試官修撰張批詞理俱稱是宜錄出
同考試官侍講彭批平順妥貼可取
考試官洗馬江批二說相須其義始備此
作得之美
考試官學士萬批義平實得旨
===
為藝為學必專其所向以究其所務焉蓋百工
之於藝君子之於學事雖殊而理則一也苟不
專所向於先究所務於後惡在其為藝為學哉
子夏之論如此謂夫事者百工之事而肆則官
府造作之處事之所由以精也工不居肆則遷
於異物而業不精然徒居肆而不精其業則亦
何益哉必安於所止而心無外慕使所為者

爲藝爲學必專其所向以究其所務焉蓋百工
之於藝君子之於學事雖殊而理則一也苟不

子夏之論如此謂夫事者百工之事而肆則官

於異物而業不精然徒居肆而不精其業則亦
□所益哉必專於所止而心無外慕使所爲者
punctuated:
第壹場
四書

「百工居肆以成其事，君子學以致其道。」
李仁傑

同考試官編修商批：能兼二說，而措詞簡當者，僅見此篇。
同考試官修撰張批：詞理俱稱是，宜錄出。
同考試官侍講彭批：平順妥貼，可取。
考試官洗馬江批：二說相須，其義始備，此作得之，美。
考試官學士萬批：義平實，得旨。

為藝、為學，必專其所向，以究其所務焉。蓋百工之於藝，君子之於學，事雖殊而理則一也。苟不專所向於先，究所務於後，惡在其為藝、為學哉？子夏之論如此。謂夫事者，百工之事；而肆則官府造作之處，事之所由以精也。工不居肆，則遷於異物而業不精；然徒居肆而不精其業，則亦何益哉？必安於所止而心無外慕，使所為者
translation_en:
First Session
The Four Books

"The hundred artisans dwell in workshops in order to accomplish their work; the gentleman learns in order to reach the utmost of his Way."
Li Renjie 李仁傑

Associate Examiner and Historiographer (Bianxiu) Shang comments: Able to combine the two interpretations while using concise and fitting phrasing—this is the only essay I have seen that does so.
Associate Examiner and Senior Compiler (Xiuzhuan) Zhang comments: Both the diction and the reasoning are well-matched and sound; it ought to be selected for publication.
Associate Examiner and Expositor-in-waiting (Shijiang) Peng comments: Smooth, balanced, and well-put; worthy of selection.
Examiner and Librarian (Xima) Jiang comments: The two interpretations depend on each other for the meaning to be complete. This composition grasps this; admirable.
Examiner and Academician (Xueshi) Wan comments: The exposition of the meaning is solid and plain, grasping the main purport.

In practicing a craft or pursuing learning, one must concentrate one's aim in order to carry one's task through to the end. For the hundred artisans in relation to their crafts, and the gentleman in relation to his learning—though their affairs differ, the principle is one and the same. If one does not first concentrate one's aim and subsequently carry one's task through to the end, wherein lies the practice of a craft or the pursuit of learning? Such was the discourse of Zixia 子夏. He meant that "work" refers to the work of the hundred artisans, while "workshops" are the places of official manufacture, whereby their work is brought to refinement. If an artisan does not dwell in a workshop, he will be distracted by extraneous things and his craft will not be refined; yet if he merely dwells in a workshop without refining his craft, of what benefit is that? He must rest settled in his place with a mind free of outside longings, causing what he makes…

title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
皆致其精良專於所治而技無他雜使所成者
皆極其工緻苟不至於精良極其工緻不止也
然子夏豈徒為百工論哉正為君子學道而發
耳盖道者當然之理而學則致知力行之事道
之所由以致也君子不學則奪於外誘而志不
篤然徒學而不致其道則亦何所得哉故必惟
日孜孜而盡致知之方於事物之所以然者有
以詣其極終日乾乾而致力行之功於事物之
所當然者有以體其全苟不詣其極不體其全
不已也吁子夏假粗以見精示人之意何深歟
論至於是則知道必由學而後造學必造道而
後成道焉非學則道自道固無得於己學不造
道則學徒學亦無以成其功君子可不知所謹
哉子夏以文學名而其言如此古人之所謂學
者可知矣
夫孝者善繼人之志善述人之事者也春
秋修其祖廟陳其宗器設其裳衣薦其時
食宗廟之禮所以序昭穆也序爵所以辨

者可知矣

皆致其精良，專於所治而技無他雜，使所成者皆極其工緻；苟不至於精良、極其工緻，不止也。然子夏豈徒為百工論哉？正為君子學道而發耳。盖道者，當然之理；而學則致知力行之事，道之所由以致也。君子不學，則奪於外誘而志不篤；然徒學而不致其道，則亦何所得哉？故必惟日孜孜而盡致知之方，於事物之所以然者，有以詣其極；終日乾乾而致力行之功，於事物之所當然者，有以體其全。苟不詣其極、不體其全，不已也。吁！子夏假粗以見精，示人之意何深歟！論至於是，則知道必由學而後造，學必造道而後成。道焉非學，則道自道，固無得於己；學不造道，則學徒學，亦無以成其功。君子可不知所謹哉？子夏以文學名，而其言如此，古人之所謂學者可知矣。

…all reach the highest quality, and to concentrate on what they work at so that their skill has no other admixture, causing everything they complete to attain the utmost fineness of workmanship; if they do not reach the highest quality and attain the utmost fineness of workmanship, they do not stop.

Yet was Zixia merely discoursing on the hundred artisans? He was precisely speaking for the sake of the gentleman learning the Way. For the Way is the principle of what ought to be, while learning is the business of extending knowledge and practicing earnestly, whereby the Way is brought to perfection. If the gentleman does not learn, he will be carried away by external enticements and his resolve will not be steadfast; yet if he merely learns without bringing the Way to perfection, what then will he gain? Therefore he must work tirelessly day by day to exhaust the method of extending knowledge, so as to reach the ultimate regarding the reasons why things and affairs are as they are; and he must be vigilant all day long to apply the effort of earnest practice, so as to embody the whole regarding what things and affairs ought to be. If he does not reach the ultimate and embody the whole, he does not cease. Ah! How profound was Zixia's intention in instructing others by borrowing the coarse to reveal the refined! When the discussion reaches this point, one knows that the Way can be attained only through learning, and learning can be completed only when it attains the Way. If there is the Way without learning, then the Way remains merely the Way on its own, and one certainly gains nothing of it for oneself; if learning does not attain the Way, then learning remains mere learning, and there is likewise no means to complete its achievement. How could the gentleman not know to be heedful of this? Zixia was renowned for culture and learning, and since his words were like this, what the ancients meant by learning can be known.

translation_en: …regard it as a hardship. Thus, not only did they praise his terrace by calling it the "Marvellous Terrace," they also delighted in the sleek does and stags reclining beneath it; not only did they praise his pond by calling it the "Marvellous Pond," they also delighted in the fish and turtles filling it and leaping within. At a single glance they rejoiced in it to such a degree—how did King Wen win this from the people? It was because his benevolent and loving heart had long won their trust amid universal harmony, and his command "not to hurry" was further proclaimed on the very day construction began. Therefore, the people who had earlier come like children to the work were now moved when gazing upon the sights: because they delighted in the joy of his terrace and pond, King Wen could relax at ease and enjoy that pleasure for a long time to come; because they delighted in the joy of his does, stags, fish, and turtles, King Wen could stroll in leisure and enjoy that pleasure without end. Had King Wen's benevolence in loving the people fallen short in any way, the people would have had aching heads and knitted brows, and many would have been unable to find their joy. And if the people could not find their joy, how could King Wen have enjoyed his pleasure alone? Thus King Wen may truly be called one who rejoiced only after the whole world rejoiced! Alas, the terraces, ponds, birds, and beasts were the same: King Wen shared his joy with the people, so the people rejoiced in it and he was able to enjoy his pleasure; Jie enjoyed his pleasure alone, so the people resented him and he could not preserve his joy. Having cited the deeds of King Wen to enlighten King Hui, Mencius went on in the following passage to point out to him the deeds of Jie; profound indeed was his intention thereby to expand Heavenly Principle, check human desires, and hold out hope for the rulers of his day. Yet what could be done when the ruler of the time was already so deeply deluded and obstinate that to the end he never awakened to it? How lamentable!

That their alternating movement never rests must have something that serves as its master—is this not also called the Way? This Way is complete within yin and operates through yang. At the moment of its operation, the Way rides upon vital force (qi) and fills the Great Void, while vital force carries principle (li) and permeates the cosmos in generative interaction; the work of transformation and nurture is pure and supremely good, and therefore it is said: "That which ensues from it is goodness." Although human beings obtain this nature in coming into life, how could they fully embody the entirety of this Way? The humane (ren) receive a preponderance of yang vital force, and so they see only the flowing and pervasive fullness of the Way and take it to be humaneness, without knowing that outside of humaneness there is what is called wisdom (zhi). Alas! Though "goodness" and "nature" differ in name, and though "humaneness" and "wisdom" vary in designation, which of them is not the operation of this Way? 諸口者言也言之誠僞出乎身若無與於民也
而民之應否頓異其加乎民也何如措諸身者
行也行之誠僞發乎邇若無與於遠也而遠之
從違頓殊其見乎遠也何似是言行也者乃君
子之樞若戶之闔闢所由關矣乃君子之機若
弩之張弛所由繫矣樞機發而當也人皆應之
榮孰甚焉發而不當也人皆違之辱孰加焉豈

===

行之僞天地以之而降殃是言行又動乎天地

觀象玩辭以致其謹哉祥殃者雖曰天降之也
實己感之也可不觀變玩占以致其慎哉吁天

人者天地之小也率性會道而形不足以囿之
則不徒求天地之天地求吾心之天地因求吾

Whether speech is sincere or false issues from one's own person, as though it had nothing to do with the people; yet whether the people respond or not is instantly different—how great is its effect upon the people! What is enacted in one's person is action. Whether action is sincere or false originates in what is near, as though it had nothing to do with what is far; yet whether those afar follow or oppose is instantly distinct—what is its manifestation afar like! Nothing is higher than Heaven, and Heaven is hard to move; nothing is thicker than Earth, and Earth is hard to move. Yet one little realizes that with the sincerity of a single word or action, Heaven and Earth thereby send down blessings; with the falsity of a single word or action, Heaven and Earth thereby send down calamities. Thus words and actions also move Heaven and Earth! punctuated: 而且考驗之，意其出於此歟？昔帝堯命羲和作曆矣，又分職頒布，而告以考驗之道。謂夫爾羲仲之官，主春時之政，測候之所在於嵎夷，而嵎夷者，東表之地也；官次之名謂之暘谷，而暘谷者，取日出之義也。彼春分初出之日，則寅敬而賓接之，以識其景，使或長或短有所考；春月所當作起之事，則均平而秩序之，使或先或後無所失。然不考驗夫日星民物，何以審其推步之當哉？是故先時而冬，日則短而星則昴也；今焉於日，則晷刻之度正適夫冬夏之中，於星，則朱鳥之宿中見於初昏之際，於以考之，而陽之中、春之仲可知矣。先時而寒，民則隩而鳥獸則氄毛也；今焉於民，則分散而處，於物，則乳化交接，於以驗之，而氣之溫、氣之和可見矣。吁！聖人於此，何其詳複之至哉！大抵天道人時，古人所甚重而不敢忽者。其推步之術，固有一定之法，而占候修改，尤致意焉。是以羲和之命，帝典攸先；璣衡之察，受終伊始。堯舜之知，夫豈無謂哉！
translation_en:
… and moreover tests and verifies it—does not the intention of the passage stem from this?

In antiquity, once Emperor Yao had commanded the Xi and He families to compile the calendar, he further divided their duties to promulgate it and instructed them in the method of verification. He said in effect: Your office, Xi Zhong, presides over the administration of the spring season. The place for your astronomical observations lies at Yuyi, and Yuyi is the land at the eastern frontier; the name of your official station is called Yanggu (Bright Valley), and Yanggu takes its meaning from the rising of the sun. As for the sun just rising at the vernal equinox, you shall respectfully welcome it as a guest in order to record its shadow, ensuring that whether the days are longer or shorter there is a basis for verification; as for the agricultural work that ought to be commenced in the spring months, you shall equalize and order it, ensuring that whether earlier or later nothing goes amiss.

Yet without testing and verifying it against the sun, the stars, the people, and living creatures, how could one judge whether the astronomical calculations are accurate? Therefore, in the preceding season of winter, the day was at its shortest and the culminating asterism was Mao (the Pleiades); now, as for the sun, the measure of day and night hits the exact midpoint between winter and summer, and as for the stars, the constellations of the Vermilion Bird appear at the meridian just at dusk. By examining these, one may know that it is the midpoint of yang and the middle month of spring. In the preceding season of cold, the people kept to the warm inner corners of their dwellings and the birds and beasts grew soft under-fur and downy feathers; now, as for the people, they disperse to dwell in the fields, and as for creatures, they breed and mate. By verifying these, one may see that the vital breath of the season is warm and harmonious.

Alas! How utterly detailed and thorough the sage was in this matter! On the whole, the Way of Heaven and the seasons of human labor were what the ancients valued most deeply and dared not neglect. While their art of astronomical calculation certainly possessed fixed methods, they paid even closer attention to observational verification and revision. For this reason, the commission to the Xi and He families stood first in the Canon of Yao, and the observation of the armillary sphere and sighting tube marked the very beginning of Shun's receiving the abdication. Was the wisdom of Yao and Shun without foundation?

刑之疑者也。刑疑，則有五罰之赦焉；正于五罰，而辭與罰參差不應，罰之疑者也。罰疑，則有五過之宥焉。然刑疑也，罰疑也，可率意為操縱哉？必推情定法，察之詳而盡其能也。若夫聽獄之道，簡核為本。茍簡核情實，可信者衆，亦惟驗之容貌，不忽于考察焉；茍情無所據，實無所得，則在所不聽，不過於尋求焉。然簡孚也，無簡也，又可恣情為取舍哉？惟天鑒有赫，不敢有毫髮之不盡也。噫！處當而必使當其法，聽察而不敢易其心，刑之用其庶乎！大抵獄者，民命之所關，國命之所關，天命之所在也。《虞書》著欽恤之訓，周文存敬忌之心，古之有國有天下者，未嘗不以之為重。政要家法，世傳代守，是以穆王訓刑，審克之說、嚴天之戒，猶惓惓焉。故余於《吕刑》，尚可想見帝王忠厚惻怛之遺意。
《詩》
「我出我車，于彼郊矣。設此旐矣，建彼旄矣。彼旟旐斯，胡不旆旆？憂心悄悄，僕夫况瘁。
translation_en:
…this is a case of doubt regarding the punishment. When the punishment is in doubt, it is commuted to one of the Five Fines. When adjudicated against the Five Fines, if the testimony and the fine are discrepant and do not correspond, this is a case of doubt regarding the fine. When the fine is in doubt, it is pardoned as one of the Five Misdemeanors. Yet whether the punishment is in doubt or the fine is in doubt, how could one arbitrarily manipulate the outcome at whim? One must infer the circumstances to determine the law, examining them in detail and exhausting one's utmost ability.

As for the way of hearing litigation, verifying the facts is fundamental. If, upon verifying the circumstances and facts, there are many points worthy of credence, one must still test them against the litigants' countenances and not be negligent in investigation. If the circumstances have no basis and no facts can be established, then the case is not to be heard, and one does not go to excess in pursuing it. Yet whether the verified facts are credible or there are no verified facts at all, how could one indulge one's own inclinations in accepting or dismissing a case? Only because Heaven's oversight is awe-inspiring does one not dare fall short by even a hair's breadth. Ah! In deciding sentences, inevitably making them match the law, and in hearing and investigating cases, not daring to take a casual attitude in one's heart—the application of punishments will then nearly reach perfection!

In general, litigation is that upon which the lives of the people depend, that upon which the destiny of the state depends, and wherein the Mandate of Heaven resides. The Book of Yu (Yushu) sets forth the instruction to be reverent and compassionate, and King Wen of Zhou preserved a heart of reverence and caution; among those in antiquity who possessed a state or possessed All under Heaven, there were none who did not regard this as weighty. As an essential of governance and a family norm, it was transmitted from generation to generation and guarded from age to age. Therefore, when King Mu gave instructions on punishments, he remained earnestly devoted to the doctrine of carefulness and diligence and the admonition to stand in awe of Heaven. Thus, in the "Punishments of Lü" (Lü xing), I can still envision the lingering intent of loyal generosity and commiseration of the former emperors and kings.

Book of Odes (Shi):
"I bring forth my carriages, out to those suburbs. I set up this tortoise-and-snake banner; I raise that yak-tail standard. Those falcon-and-tortoise banners—do they not flutter wavingly? Yet my sorrowful heart is deeply anxious, and the grooms are all the more worn out. …"

Comment by Associate Examiner, Vice Director Huang: Readers of the Book of Odes (Shi) often force their own private views onto passages that are plain and straightforward. This essay is recorded here to serve as a standard model.

Comment by Associate Examiner, Examining Editor Wu: In depicting Nanzhong's cautious apprehension and his rousing martial spirit, the diction does not lapse into florid extravagance. An essay like this in the examination compound is truly like the sound of footsteps in a deserted valley!

Comment by Associate Examiner, Senior Compiler Luo: In the examination compound, essays written on the "Sending Forth the Chariots" ("Chuche") topic were, if not trite, then offensively bizarre and convoluted. For refined diction and clear meaning, this piece ought to be selected.

Comment by Examiner, Librarian Jiang: The essay brings forth genuine insight; he is truly a skilled writer.

Comment by Examiner, Academician Wan: It captures the spirit of comforting and rewarding the returning commander at the time; it is fitting that this be recorded and published.

When a true king rewards a returning commander for his toil, he first recounts how, upon leading forth the army, the commander maintained a heart of cautious apprehension, and then recounts how, in carrying out his mandate, he achieved a record of rousing martial success. For in the essentials of conducting a military campaign, nothing takes precedence over cautious apprehension, and nothing is more prized than rousing martial vigor. When a great general is able to fulfill both of these, how could a true king fail to recount them in rewarding him upon his return?

title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
之旐亦建之以揔夫師旅彼鳥隼之旟豈不旆
旆然而飛揚乎所建之旐又不旆旆然而輕舉
乎但將帥方以責任為憂而憂懼之莫遑也僕
夫亦以攻戰為憂而憔悴之不已也夫出師而
有戒懼之心如此則其奮揚之威從可知矣彼
南仲以王朝之名將為三軍之統御上承王命
往城朔方其所出之車既彭彭然而眾盛所建
之旂旐又央央然而鮮明斯時也出師之意南
仲固已知之而軍眾猶未之知於是傳王命以
===
令之若曰天子命我出師于邁非欲窮兵也以
玁狁侵陵使城彼朔方以禦之耳非欲黷武也
使往城朔方以備玁狁之侵陵耳然此南仲威
名之赫然固已震驚乎朔方之境繹騷于醜虜
之庭彼蕞尔玁狁之患豈不蕩然而遂除靡然
而于襄乎奮揚之威又若此非其先存戒懼之
心曷能然哉吁若南仲之用兵可謂得靜翕動
闢之道者矣大抵將兵在將將將在君將之將
兵固當思所以建其功君之將將尤當知所以

punctuated: 之旐亦建之以揔夫師旅。彼鳥隼之旟，豈不旆旆然而飛揚乎？所建之旐，又不旆旆然而輕舉乎？但將帥方以責任為憂，而憂懼之莫遑也；僕夫亦以攻戰為憂，而憔悴之不已也。夫出師而有戒懼之心如此，則其奮揚之威從可知矣。彼南仲以王朝之名將，為三軍之統御，上承王命，往城朔方。其所出之車，既彭彭然而眾盛；所建之旂旐，又央央然而鮮明。斯時也，出師之意，南仲固已知之，而軍眾猶未之知。於是傳王命以令之，若曰：「天子命我出師于邁，非欲窮兵也，以玁狁侵陵，使城彼朔方以禦之耳；非欲黷武也，使往城朔方以備玁狁之侵陵耳。」然此南仲威名之赫然，固已震驚乎朔方之境，繹騷于醜虜之庭，彼蕞尔玁狁之患，豈不蕩然而遂除、靡然而于襄乎？奮揚之威又若此，非其先存戒懼之心，曷能然哉！吁！若南仲之用兵，可謂得靜翕動闢之道者矣。大抵將兵在將，將將在君。將之將兵，固當思所以建其功；君之將將，尤當知所以
translation_en:
… the yak-tail standard [written 旐 for 旄] was likewise raised to marshal the hosts and brigades. Did not that falcon-emblazoned banner flutter and soar aloft? And did not the tortoise-and-serpent standard that had been raised wave lightly in the wind? Yet the commander was just then burdened with anxiety over his heavy responsibility, having no leisure from his worry and dread; and the charioteers and grooms, too, were anxious over the impending battles, growing ever more haggard and worn. Now, since at the dispatch of the army he possessed such a mind of caution and dread, the awe-inspiring might of his spirited martial display could readily be known from this.

That Nan Zhong, as a renowned general of the royal court and commander-in-chief of the three armies, received the king's charge from above to go forth and fortify the Northern Region (Shuofang). The war chariots he led out were already rumbling and numerous in their multitude, and the dragon-and-bell standards and tortoise-and-serpent banners he raised were bright and resplendent. At that moment, the purpose of dispatching the army was of course already known to Nan Zhong, yet the mass of the troops did not yet know it. Thereupon he transmitted the king's command to instruct them, as if to say: "The Son of Heaven has commanded us to lead the army on the march—not because he wishes to exhaust military force, but because the Xianyun are encroaching and harassing us, so he sends us to fortify that Northern Region simply to ward them off; not because he wishes to indulge in martial aggression, but simply to send us to go and fortify the Northern Region in order to guard against the encroachments of the Xianyun." Yet the illustriousness of this Nan Zhong's awe-inspiring reputation had already sent shockwaves across the borders of the Northern Region and thrown the court of the vile caitiffs into turmoil; how could the menace of those petty Xianyun not be swept clean away and utterly dispelled and overcome? That the might of his spirited display was also like this—had he not first harbored a mind of caution and dread, how could it have been so?

Ah! Conducted as Nan Zhong conducted his campaigns, the art of war may truly be said to have attained the Way of contraction in stillness and expansion in movement. On the whole, commanding soldiers rests with the general, while commanding generals rests with the ruler. When a general commands soldiers, he must certainly ponder how to establish his merit; when a ruler commands generals, he must especially know how to…

…reward their achievements. On the day their generals and commanders returned in triumph, the former kings of Zhou recounted their feelings to console and reward them. In one instance they said, "The King's business has many difficulties, and it is urgent indeed!" In another they said, "With hearts deeply anxious, the grooms and drivers are worn out all the more." title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
然言表錄之
王者之於大臣勉以世功而期報之也深錫以
策命而寵異之也至甚矣宣王得待世臣之體
也方其勸功而即期報之及其賞功而又寵異
之是宜詩人作歌以敘其事歟昔宣王命召虎
之往江漢而勉之若曰昔我文武誕膺景命當
時有如召公任夾輔之勞而闢國百里寔為我
周之翰矣盡篤棐之忠以宣化南國寔為我周
之榦矣今汝以元勳之裔為小子之臣江漢未
===
平則命汝以經營四方無曰以予小子之故但
自為嗣汝召公闢國之事耳江漢既平則命汝
以徹我疆土亦無曰以予小子之故但自為纘
汝召公宣化之業耳且能開敏汝功無忝於召
公前日之功則我祉福之錫亦不異乎文武前
日之錫期報之也不其深乎迨夫虎功告成策
命之賜不容緩也彼圭瓚秬鬯用之王廟者也
必釐爾圭瓚秬鬯一卣使得以祀其先祖焉山
川土田以待有功者也必告于文人錫山土田

然言表錄之
王者之於大臣勉以世功而期報之也深錫以
策命而寵異之也至甚矣宣王得待世臣之體
也方其勸功而即期報之及其賞功而又寵異
之是宜詩人作歌以叙其事歟昔宣王命召虎
之往江漢而勉之若曰昔我文武誕膺景命當
時有如召公任夾輔之勞而闢國百里寔爲我
周之翰矣盡篤棐之忠以宣化南國寔爲我周
之榦矣今汝以元勳之裔爲小子之臣江漢未
===
平則命汝以經營四方無曰以予小子之故但
自爲嗣汝召公闢國之事耳江漢既平則命汝
以徹我疆土亦無曰以予小子之故但自爲纘
汝召公宣化之業耳且能開敏汝功無忝於召
公前日之功則我祉福之錫亦不異乎文武前
日之錫期報之也不其深乎迨夫虎功告成禁
命之賜不容緩也彼圭瓚秬鬯用之王廟者也
必釐爾圭瓚秬鬯一卣使得以祀其先祖焉山
川土田以待有功者也必告于文人錫山土田
punctuated:
然言表，錄之。
王者之於大臣，勉以世功而期報之也深，錫以策命而寵異之也至。甚矣，宣王得待世臣之體也！方其勸功而即期報之，及其賞功而又寵異之，是宜詩人作歌以敘其事歟！昔宣王命召虎之往江、漢而勉之，若曰：昔我文、武誕膺景命，當時有如召公，任夾輔之勞，而闢國百里，寔為我周之翰矣；盡篤棐之忠，以宣化南國，寔為我周之榦矣。今汝以元勳之裔，為小子之臣，江、漢未平，則命汝以經營四方，無曰以予小子之故，但自為嗣汝召公闢國之事耳；江、漢既平，則命汝以徹我疆土，亦無曰以予小子之故，但自為纘汝召公宣化之業耳。且能開敏汝功，無忝於召公前日之功，則我祉福之錫，亦不異乎文、武前日之錫，期報之也不其深乎！迨夫虎功告成，策命之賜不容緩也。彼圭瓚、秬鬯，用之王廟者也，必釐爾圭瓚、秬鬯一卣，使得以祀其先祖焉；山川、土田，以待有功者也，必告于文人，錫山、土田，
translation_en:
… clearly beyond the words themselves. Record it for publication.

When a true king deals with his great ministers, he exhorts them with the achievements of their ancestors and promises to reward them deeply; he bestows upon them charges of investiture and favors them with the utmost distinction. Indeed, King Xuan (Xuanwang 宣王) truly grasped the proper way of treating hereditary ministers! Just as he was encouraging their meritorious service, he already promised to reward them; and when it came time to reward their merit, he further favored them with special distinction. How fitting it was that the poet composed a song to recount this affair!

In the past, when King Xuan commanded Shao Hu 召虎 to go to the Jiang 江 and Han 漢 rivers, he exhorted him as if to say: "In former times, when our Kings Wen 文 and Wu 武 grandly received the glorious mandate, there was at that time one such as the Duke of Shao (Shaogong 召公), who bore the toil of assisting the royal house and opened up the state by a hundred li, truly serving as a bulwark for our Zhou 周 dynasty; and who exhausted his staunch, supportive loyalty to spread transformative teachings through the southern states, truly serving as a pillar for our Zhou dynasty. Now you, as the descendant of that foremost meritorious minister, serve as minister to me, the Little Child. While the Jiang and Han regions are not yet pacified, I command you to bring order to the four quarters—do not say it is for the sake of me, the Little Child, but simply take it upon yourself to carry on your ancestor the Duke of Shao's work of opening up the state. Once the Jiang and Han regions are pacified, I command you to lay out the tax divisions of our territory—again, do not say it is for the sake of me, the Little Child, but simply take it upon yourself to continue your ancestor the Duke of Shao's enterprise of spreading transformative teachings. Moreover, if you are able to briskly unfold your merits so as not to disgrace the former merits of the Duke of Shao, then my bestowal of blessings and felicity will likewise be no different from the former bestowals of Kings Wen and Wu." Was not his promise of reward deep indeed?

When Hu's meritorious work was proclaimed complete, the bestowal of the charge of investiture brooked no delay. Now, the jade-handled libation ladle and black-millet aromatic wine are things used in the royal ancestral temple; yet the king unfailingly granted him a jade-handled libation ladle and a jar of black-millet aromatic wine, so that he might sacrifice to his ancestors… The mountains, rivers, lands, and fields are reserved for those of merit; thus the king unfailingly announced it to the accomplished ancestors and bestowed upon him mountains, lands, and fields, …

title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
使得以廣其封邑焉又念岐周為我祖文王始
興之地而爾祖召公受命之所故又俾往岐周
受此休命于以彰我國家之有世臣勳業赫如
而後先相望也于以昭爾召祖之有賢胤寵命
渥如而奕葉相承也寵異之也不其至乎載考
宣王之世率用世臣平淮夷也則命召虎平徐
方也則命皇父召虎念康公卒致江漢之平皇
父念南仲卒為南國之惠其所以復文武之境
土隆中興之業者蓋有自矣然亦豈非文武棫
樸豐芑之化累世培植之明驗歟
春秋
元年春王正月隱公元年
吳郁

…so that he might thereby enlarge his enfeoffed domain. Furthermore, bearing in mind that Qizhou was the place where our ancestor King Wen first rose to prominence, and where your ancestor Duke Shao received his charge, he therefore also bade him go to Qizhou to receive this beneficent mandate. By this he made manifest that our state possesses hereditary ministers whose meritorious achievements shine brilliantly, looking upon one another from past to present; by this he demonstrated that your ancestor Shao possesses a worthy descendant upon whom favored mandates are richly bestowed, passed down through successive generations. Was not the favor and distinction shown to him reaching the utmost degree? When we further examine the reign of King Xuan, he generally employed hereditary ministers: to pacify the Huai Yi, he commanded Shao Hu; to pacify the region of Xu, he commanded Huangfu. Shao Hu remained mindful of Duke Kang and ultimately brought about the pacification of the Jiang and Han rivers; Huangfu remained mindful of Nanzhong and ultimately became a benefactor to the southern states. That whereby he recovered the territory of Kings Wen and Wu and exalted the enterprise of restoration indeed had its source. Yet is this not also a clear proof of the transforming influence of Kings Wen and Wu—celebrated in the odes "Yupu" and "Fengqi"—nurtured and cultivated over successive generations?

Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)

"First year, spring, the king's first month." [First year of Duke Yin]

Wu Yu 吳郁

title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
作之意故特錄之
體乾坤之用以紀年者法乎古制明天人之理
以紀月者裁自聖心此孔子修經之功所以為
大也慨夫世入春秋王者之迹既熄諸侯之政
無統幸而天生孔子有德無位假魯史以修春
秋因衰世而立治法於隱公即位之始年不曰
一年而謂之元年者盖以大哉乾元萬物資始
天之用也欲人君上體乾元之德以養萬民至
哉坤元萬物資生地之用也欲人君下體坤元
===
之德以育萬民如此則與天地參而人君之用
行矣稽之舜典有元日之紀商訓有元祀之稱
而此書元年乃祖二帝明三王述而不作者也
至於紀月而以正次王王次春者盖以王者不
承天則無以行號令於天下故必欽若昊天而
罔違諸侯不奉王則無以施政教於國中故必
謹守王度而弗畔如此則各成其德而天人之理
明矣考之虞夏商周之書書時不繫月書月不
冠時而此書春王正月乃立法創制裁自聖心

作之意故特錄出一
體乾坤之用以紀年者法乎古制明天人之理
以紀月者裁自聖心此孔子修經之功所以為
大也〔嘅夫世入春秋王者之迹既熄諸侯之政〕
無統孝而天生孔子有德無位假魯史以修春
秋因衰世而立治法於隱公即位之始年不曰
一年而謂之元年者蓋以大哉乾元萬物資始
天之用也欲人君上體乾元之德以養萬民至
哉坤元萬物資生地之用也欲人君下體坤元
===
之德以育萬民如此則與天地參而人君之用
行矣稽之舜典有元日之紀商訓有元祀之稱
而此書元年乃祖二帝明三王述而不作者也
至於紀月而以正次王王次春者蓋以王者不
承天則無以行號令於天下故必欽若昊天而
罔違諸侯不奉王則無以施政教於國中故必
謹守王度而弗畔如此則各成其德而天人之理
明矣考之虞夏商周之書書時不繫月書月不
冠時而此書春王正月乃立法創制裁自聖心
punctuated:
作之意，故特錄之。

體乾坤之用以紀年者，法乎古制；明天人之理以紀月者，裁自聖心。此孔子修經之功所以為大也。慨夫世入春秋，王者之迹既熄，諸侯之政無統。幸而天生孔子，有德無位，假魯史以修《春秋》，因衰世而立治法。於隱公即位之始年，不曰一年而謂之元年者，盖以「大哉乾元，萬物資始」，天之用也，欲人君上體乾元之德以養萬民；「至哉坤元，萬物資生」，地之用也，欲人君下體坤元之德以育萬民。如此，則與天地參，而人君之用行矣。稽之《舜典》有「元日」之紀，《商訓》有「元祀」之稱，而此書「元年」，乃祖二帝、明三王，述而不作者也。至於紀月，而以「正」次「王」、「王」次「春」者，盖以王者不承天，則無以行號令於天下，故必欽若昊天而罔違；諸侯不奉王，則無以施政教於國中，故必謹守王度而弗畔。如此，則各成其德，而天人之理明矣。考之虞、夏、商、周之書，書時不繫月，書月不冠時，而此書「春王正月」，乃立法創制，裁自聖心，
translation_en:
…and creating, and therefore we have specially recorded it.

Embodying the functions of Qian and Kun to record the year follows ancient institutions; illuminating the principles of Heaven and humanity to record the month was determined by the mind of the Sage. This is why Confucius's achievement in compiling the Classic is so great. Alas, when the world entered the Spring and Autumn period, the traces of the true king had died out, and the governance of the feudal lords lacked unity. Fortunately, Heaven gave birth to Confucius, who possessed virtue without holding office; he borrowed the history of Lu to compile the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu), establishing laws of governance out of an age of decline. Regarding the initial year of Duke Yin's accession, the reason it is not called the "one year" but is termed the "primal year" (yuannian) is that "Great indeed is the primal power of Qian (Qianyuan); all things owe their beginning to it"—this is the function of Heaven, and he wished the ruler of men above to embody the virtue of the primal power of Qian so as to nourish the myriad people; "Utmost indeed is the primal power of Kun (Kunyuan); all things owe their birth to it"—this is the function of Earth, and he wished the ruler of men below to embody the virtue of the primal power of Kun so as to nurture the myriad people. When it is thus, he forms a triad with Heaven and Earth, and the function of the ruler of men is carried out. Examining the Canon of Shun (Shundian), there is the record of the "primal day" (yuanri), and in the Instructions of Shang (Shangxun), there is the designation of the "primal sacrificial year" (yuansi); in writing "primal year" here, he took the Two Emperors as ancestors and illuminated the Three Kings, transmitting without creating. As for recording the month, the reason he placed "first [month]" (zheng) after "King" (wang), and "King" after "Spring" (chun), is that if the true king does not receive his mandate from Heaven, he has no means to issue commands and orders throughout the realm, and thus he must reverently accord with vast Heaven and never disobey; if the feudal lords do not honor the king, they have no means to implement governance and instruction within their states, and thus they must carefully observe the royal regulations and never rebel. When it is thus, each accomplishes his virtue, and the principles of Heaven and humanity are made clear. Examining the documents of Yu, Xia, Shang, and Zhou, when they wrote the season they did not attach the month, and when they wrote the month they did not prefix the season; in writing "Spring, the King's first month" here, he established laws and created institutions, determining them from the mind of the Sage,…

無所述於人者也吁述於人以立萬世常行之
道作於已以寓百王不易之法一述一作之間而

經之功殆不止此二百四十二年之間叙先後之
倫而五典以惇秩上下之分而五禮以庸有德

無所述於人者也。吁！述於人以立萬世常行之道，作於已以寓百王不易之法，一述一作之間，而大義寓焉。故曰：「《春秋》非聖人莫能修。」抑聖人修經之功，殆不止此。二百四十二年之間，叙先後之倫，而五典以惇；秩上下之分，而五禮以庸。有德者必褒，而善自此可勸；有罪者必貶，而惡自此可懲。信不易之宏軌，傳心之要典也。先儒謂其志存乎經世，其功配於抑洪水、膺戎狄、放龍蛇、驅虎豹，其大要則皆天子之事也，信夫！

公及齊侯、宋公、陳侯、衛侯、鄭伯、許男、曹伯會王世子于首止〔僖公五年〕；叔孫僑如會晉士燮、齊高無咎、宋華元、衛孫林父、鄭公子鰌、邾人會吳于鍾離〔成公十五年〕；公會晉侯、宋公、衛侯、曹伯、莒子、邾子、滕子、薛伯、杞伯、小邾子、齊世子光會吳于柤〔襄公十年〕；季孫宿、叔老會晉士匄、齊人、宋人、衛人、鄭公孫蠆、〔曹人〕、莒人、邾人、滕人、薛人、杞人、小邾人會吳于向〔襄公十四年〕。
translation_en:
…without transmitting anything from others. Ah! By transmitting from others, he established the constant Way to be practiced for ten thousand generations; by creating from himself, he lodged therein the unchangeable laws for a hundred kings. Between this one act of transmitting and one act of creating, the great principles are lodged. Therefore it is said: "None but a sage could have compiled the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)." Yet the sage's achievement in compiling the Classic scarcely stops at this. Across two hundred and forty-two years, he ordered the human relationships according to priority, and thereby the Five Canons of social duty were strengthened; he regulated the distinctions between superior and inferior, and thereby the Five Rites were put into practice. Those who possessed virtue were invariably praised, so that from this goodness could be encouraged; those who committed offenses were invariably censured, so that from this evil could be deterred. Truly it is an immutable grand standard and an essential canon for transmitting the mind of the sages! Former scholars said that his aspiration lay in ordering the world, that his achievement matched those of repressing the floodwaters, repelling the Rong and Di barbarians, banishing dragons and snakes, and driving away tigers and leopards, and that in its essential import these are all the affairs of the Son of Heaven. Truly it is so!

"The Duke, together with the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Zheng, the Baron of Xu, and the Earl of Cao, met with the Royal Heir Apparent at Shouzhi" [fifth year of Duke Xi]; "Shusun Qiaoru joined Shi Xie of Jin, Gao Wujiu of Qi, Hua Yuan of Song, Sun Linfu of Wei, Gongzi Qiu of Zheng, and a man of Zhu in meeting with Wu at Zhongli" [fifteenth year of Duke Cheng]; "The Duke joined the Marquis of Jin, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Cao, the Viscount of Ju, the Viscount of Zhu, the Viscount of Teng, the Earl of Xue, the Earl of Qi, the Viscount of Lesser Zhu, and Heir Apparent Guang of Qi in meeting with Wu at Zha" [tenth year of Duke Xiang]; "Jisun Su and Shu Lao joined Shi Gai of Jin, a man of Qi, a man of Song, a man of Wei, Gongsun Chai of Zheng, [a man of Cao], a man of Ju, a man of Zhu, a man of Teng, a man of Xue, a man of Qi, and a man of Lesser Zhu in meeting with Wu at Xiang" [fourteenth year of Duke Xiang].

《春秋》既正君臣之分，尤謹華夷之辨。甚矣，《春秋》為正名分作也，得不於齊桓之會世子、晉伯之會吳人，而殊詞以致意哉？且夫君臣之分所當正也。有如齊桓因惠王溺愛，儲位未安，當世子之下臨，講首止之好會，明長幼之序，摅翼戴之誠，則叔帶之謀遂息，而大本之位定矣。聖人修經，盖謂世子，君也；諸侯，臣也。以王世子而下會諸侯，則陵；以諸侯而上與王世子會，則抗。下陵上替，不可以訓。故於是役，特書「及以會」者，使若
translation_en:
Liu Fengxiang 劉鳳翔

Associate Examiner Examining Editor Zhang comments: "Rectifying the relationship between ruler and subject and strictly maintaining the distinction between barbarian and Chinese are the grand principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu). This composition grasps them."
Associate Examiner Junior Compiler Jiao comments: "The Sage lodged the successes and failures of Qi and Jin within his historiographical phrasing. This composition brings them to light, and its prose is moreover detailed and well-ordered; it is worthy of recording."
Examiner Librarian Jiang comments: "He is able to synthesize the ideas of the former Confucians, which suffices to show that he has applied his mind earnestly to the commentaries."
Examiner Academician Wan comments: "It articulates the intent of the Spring and Autumn Annals in strictly maintaining the distinctions between ruler and subject and between barbarian and Chinese; it may be selected."

The Spring and Autumn Annals not only rectifies the distinction between ruler and subject, but takes even greater care in maintaining the differentiation between Chinese and barbarian. Profound indeed is the fact that the Spring and Autumn Annals was composed to rectify names and status obligations! How could it not employ distinctive phrasing to convey its intent regarding Huan of Qi's meeting with the Royal Heir Apparent and the hegemons of Jin's meetings with the men of Wu?

Now, the distinction between ruler and subject is something that must be rectified. Take, for instance, Huan of Qi: because King Hui indulged in偏愛 (doting favoritism) and the position of the heir apparent was not yet secure, when the Heir Apparent condescendingly came down, Huan conducted the friendly meeting at Shouzhi, clarifying the order of elder and younger and pouring forth his sincerity in supporting and upholding him; thereupon the schemes of Shu Dai ceased, and the position of the great foundation of the state was settled. When the Sage compiled the Classic, he surely considered that the Heir Apparent is in the position of ruler, whereas the feudal lords are subjects. For the Royal Heir Apparent to condescend to meet with the feudal lords below is an encroachment from below; for the feudal lords to presume to meet as equals with the Royal Heir Apparent above is defiance. When the lower encroaches and the upper is diminished, it cannot serve as instruction. Therefore, regarding this affair, he specially wrote "and so met with" (ji yi hui 及以會), making it appear as though…

title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
王世子在是諸侯咸往會焉意在尊王室不敢
與世子抗也其正君臣之分為何如若夫華夷
之辨所當謹也夫何晉因楚患數興資吳制楚
厲也既會吳于鍾離悼也兩會吳于柤向以中
國冠帶之君結短髮文身之夷則困楚之策未
行而吳人之勢張矣聖人修經盖謂晉華夏也
吳夷狄也以諸夏而親遠人則失序以遠人而
交諸夏則亂常内弱外強不可以示故於是三
役特書會以會者使若諸侯在是吳人來與會
===
焉意在賤夷狄罪諸侯不敢與之敵也其謹華
夷之辨又何如抑春秋書法之嚴不特此也他
如王以諸侯伐鄭則書諸侯從王晉文會温召
君則書天王自狩皆所以尊君抑臣也宋虢之
後楚黃池之先晉非所以貴夏賤夷乎噫君臣
既正則西周之往轍可尋夷夏既明則膺懲之
家法猶在聖人拳拳扶持世道之意不亦深切
著明也哉
禮記

punctuated:
王世子在是，諸侯咸往會焉，意在尊王室，不敢與世子抗也。其正君臣之分為何如？若夫華夷之辨，所當謹也。夫何晉因楚患數興，資吳制楚，厲也既會吳于鍾離，悼也兩會吳于柤、向。以中國冠帶之君，結短髮文身之夷，則困楚之策未行，而吳人之勢張矣。聖人修經，盖謂晉，華夏也；吳，夷狄也。以諸夏而親遠人則失序，以遠人而交諸夏則亂常。内弱外強，不可以示，故於是三役，特書「會以會」者，使若諸侯在是，吳人來與會焉，意在賤夷狄、罪諸侯，不敢與之敵也。其謹華夷之辨又何如？抑《春秋》書法之嚴，不特此也。他如王以諸侯伐鄭，則書「諸侯從王」；晉文會温召君，則書「天王自狩」，皆所以尊君抑臣也。宋、虢之後楚，黃池之先晉，非所以貴夏賤夷乎？噫！君臣既正，則西周之往轍可尋；夷夏既明，則膺懲之家法猶在。聖人拳拳扶持世道之意，不亦深切著明也哉！
禮記
translation_en:
…the Royal Heir Apparent was present there, and the feudal lords all went to meet with him—the intention being to honor the royal house and not dare to stand as equals to the Heir Apparent. How great indeed was this rectification of the distinction between ruler and subject!

As for the differentiation between Chinese and barbarian, that too must be carefully guarded. Why then did Jin, because the threat from Chu repeatedly arose, rely on Wu to check Chu, so that Duke Li first met with Wu at Zhongli, and Duke Dao twice met with Wu at Zha and Xiang? For capped and sashed rulers of the Central States to ally themselves with short-haired, tattooed barbarians meant that before the strategy to hem in Chu could even be carried out, the power of the people of Wu had already grown formidable. When the Sage compiled the Classic, he surely considered that Jin was of the Chinese states (Huaxia), whereas Wu was of the barbarian tribes (Yidi). For the Chinese states to draw close to distant peoples violates proper order; for distant peoples to consort with the Chinese states disrupts constant norms. Weakness within and strength without could not be held up as a model. Therefore, in recording these three campaigns, he specially wrote "met in order to meet with," making it appear as though the feudal lords were present there and the people of Wu came to join the meeting with them—his intention being to disparage the barbarians and fault the feudal lords, not daring to treat them as peers. How great too was this careful guarding of the differentiation between Chinese and barbarian!

Moreover, the strictness of the historiographical principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) is not limited to these instances alone. In other cases—such as when the King led the feudal lords to attack Zheng, it records that "the feudal lords followed the King"; and when Duke Wen of Jin summoned his ruler to the meeting at Wen, it records that "the Heavenly King went hunting of his own accord"—all such entries serve to honor the ruler and restrain the subject. Putting Chu after at the meetings of Song and Guo, and placing Jin first at the meeting of Huangchi—was this not the means to esteem the Chinese and disparage the barbarians?

Alas! Once the relation between ruler and subject is rectified, the former tracks of the Western Zhou can be retraced; once the distinction between barbarian and Chinese is made clear, the dynastic tradition of smiting and punishing transgressors still endures. Is not the Sage's earnest intention to uphold the moral order of the world both profound and manifest!

Record of Rites (Liji)

論人之生，稟造化理氣而獨得其秀也。蓋人者，天地間一物耳，然非得造化理氣之秀，其何以靈於萬物哉？且夫天之所生，地之所養，無人為大。人也者，何為獨得其秀邪？是故天地之道，一陰一陽而已。彼曰元、曰亨，實理之健而陽也，人則得之為仁、為禮焉；曰利、曰貞，實理之順而陰
translation_en:
"Therefore, man is the virtue of Heaven and Earth, the interaction of yin and yang, the convergence of ghosts and spirits, and the finest vital force of the Five Phases."

Xiang Min 項旻

Associate Examiner Secretary Bi 畢 comments: Students of the Rites are generally able to discuss this in terms of principle (li) and vital force (qi), yet only this paper explains how human beings alone obtain the finest of principle and vital force. Moreover, in expounding and threading together yin and yang, each section follows seamlessly from the last with its own subtle excellence. How could the red-robed spirit of examinations not nod in approval at it?
Associate Examiner Supervising Secretary Yang 楊 comments: Former Confucians said that this passage is the purest essence, yet many who rush to explicate it remain blind to its true purport. Only this essay integrates principle into composition, clearly sketching out a Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate. Worthy of selection.
Examiner Librarian Jiang 江 comments: The composition and reasoning are balanced and solid.
Examiner Academician Wan 萬 comments: The explication grasps the main purport.

This discusses how human life is endowed with the principle and vital force of creation and alone obtains their finest essence. Now, man is merely one creature between Heaven and Earth; yet were he not endowed with the finest of creation's principle and vital force, how could he be the most sentient of the myriad things? Moreover, among all that Heaven generates and Earth nourishes, none is greater than man. Why is it that man alone obtains their finest essence? Therefore, the Way of Heaven and Earth is nothing more than yin and yang. What are called origination (yuan) and flourishing (heng) are the vigor of real principle, which is yang; man obtains them to become benevolence and propriety. What are called advantage (li) and firmness (zhen) are the compliance of real principle, which is yin…

title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
也人則得之為義為智焉既得是理以為性必
得是氣以成形形之始也陰之所合而形以成
有形斯有氣氣之始也陽之所變而氣以聚有
氣斯有形形則陰而陰之靈者為鬼體魄屬焉
氣則陽而陽之靈者為神魂氣屬焉凡呼吸寤
寐之間一鬼神之妙合凡語默動靜之際一鬼
神之凝聚是以其形之所以生不偏而塞得五
行至陰之精而最秀也其神之所以發不駁而
雜得五行至陽之精而最粹也吁所謂人者物
===
之至也良有以夫雖然人固秀於天地之間而
靈於物矣而聖人之生則又得其秀之秀者故
能踐形盡性與天地合其德日月合其明四時
合其序鬼神合其吉凶此其所以成位乎中而
又為人之至也歟
故君子多聞質而守之多志質而親之精
知畧而行之

也，人則得之為義、為智焉。既得是理以為性，必得是氣以成形。形之始也，陰之所合而形以成，有形斯有氣；氣之始也，陽之所變而氣以聚，有氣斯有形。形則陰，而陰之靈者為鬼，體魄屬焉；氣則陽，而陽之靈者為神，魂氣屬焉。凡呼吸寤寐之間，一鬼神之妙合；凡語默動靜之際，一鬼神之凝聚。是以其形之所以生，不偏而塞，得五行至陰之精而最秀也；其神之所以發，不駁而雜，得五行至陽之精而最粹也。吁！所謂「人者，物之至也」，良有以夫！雖然，人固秀於天地之間而靈於物矣，而聖人之生，則又得其秀之秀者。故能踐形盡性，與天地合其德，日月合其明，四時合其序，鬼神合其吉凶。此其所以成位乎中，而又為人之至也歟！

「故君子多聞，質而守之；多志，質而親之；精知，畧而行之。」

translation_en:
… and humans obtain these to become their righteousness and their wisdom. Having obtained this principle as their nature, they must obtain this vital force to form their physical body. At the beginning of physical form, yin coalesces and the form is completed; where there is form, there is vital force. At the beginning of vital force, yang transforms and the vital force gathers; where there is vital force, there is physical form. Form is yin, and the numinous efficacy of yin is the earthly spirit (gui), to which the bodily vitality (tipo) belongs; vital force is yang, and the numinous efficacy of yang is the heavenly spirit (shen), to which the spiritual breath (hunqi) belongs. Every moment of breathing, waking, and sleeping is entirely the marvelous union of gui and shen; every occasion of speaking, keeping silent, moving, and resting is entirely the condensation and gathering of gui and shen. Therefore, that by which one's physical form is generated is neither one-sided nor obstructed, having obtained the essence of the utmost yin of the Five Phases and being the most refined; that by which one's spirit is manifested is neither impure nor mixed, having obtained the essence of the utmost yang of the Five Phases and being the purest. Ah! When it is said that "humans are the ultimate of things," there is truly good reason for it! Even so, while humans are indeed the finest presence between Heaven and Earth and the most numinous of creatures, the birth of a sage obtains the very finest of that finest essence. Thus the sage is able to fulfill his physical form and exhaust his nature, matching his virtue with Heaven and Earth, his brilliance with the sun and moon, his order with the four seasons, and his auspicious and inauspicious workings with the spirits (guishen). Is this not how he establishes his position in the center, and in turn becomes the ultimate of humankind?

"Therefore, the gentleman hears much, verifies it, and holds fast to it; he remembers much, verifies it, and stays close to it; he refines his knowledge, summarizes it, and puts it into practice." [Book of Rites, Biaoji]
By Jiang Rong 蔣容.

君子之事上也，資衆論而有得，思至約而後行。蓋人臣事君，以謀政爲先。苟資之於衆而有得焉，又可不思其約以見於用哉？此《緇衣》篇論義壹行類之道如此。謂夫人臣之事上也，言無物則義斯不一，行無格則行斯無類。欲義壹而行類，可不廣聞見爲之資乎？彼嘉謀嘉猷，凡可以啓沃吾君者，聞非不多也；然猶不敢自是，必正於衆人而可否之。庶言同則言爲有物，斯服膺而勿失矣。善政善教，凡可以膏澤吾民者，見非不廣也；然猶不敢自是，必質於多士而參挹之。

… effort. This essay is able to establish its argument based on the surrounding context so as to dispel general doubts; he is a scholar well-versed through study and discussion. I recommend it.
Comment by Associate Examiner Supervising Secretary Yang: This composition sets up its argument around taking counsel in governance, while the principle of serving one's superior overflows beyond the words. Moreover, his papers across all three sessions are well-matched; taking him to head my examination ward is fitting indeed.
Comment by Examiner Librarian Jiang: Does not lose the original purport, and its analysis is detailed and clear—truly an outstanding piece among the Record of Rites (Liji) essays.
Comment by Examiner Academician Wan: Both diction and reasoning are concise and clear.

In serving his superior, the gentleman draws upon the discussions of the multitude to gain understanding, and reflects until he reaches what is most essential before acting. Indeed, when a minister serves his lord, he puts taking counsel for governance first. If he draws upon the multitude and gains something thereby, how can he not reflect upon what is essential so as to manifest it in practice? Such is the way of "unified righteousness and consistent conduct" discussed in the "Black Robes" (Ziyi) chapter. It means that when a minister serves his superior, if his words lack substance, then his righteousness will not be unified; if his conduct lacks a standard, then his conduct will have no consistency. If one desires that righteousness be unified and conduct consistent, can one fail to broaden what one hears and sees as a resource for it? As for those fine counsels and admirable plans—whatever can enlighten and enrich our lord—what he has heard of them is by no means little; yet he still dares not consider himself right, and must verify them with the multitude to judge what is acceptable or not. When common opinion agrees, his words have substance, and thus he clasps them to his breast without losing them. As for good governance and good instruction—whatever can bring nourishing blessings to our people—what he has seen of them is by no means narrow; yet he still dares not consider himself right, and must verify them with the many scholars to compare and draw from them. …

translation_en:
…When public opinion is in accord, one's actions possess a standard, and thus one pursues inquiry and learning without tiring. Now, when what one has heard and seen is already extensive, it can certainly serve as a resource for one's words and actions. Yet amidst much hearing, there is not necessarily no succinct essence; one must further carefully ponder what is most succinct within it and apply it to one's counsel and advice, so that one's words do not err on the side of tediousness and importunity, and may thereby benefit our sovereign. Amidst much seeing, there is not necessarily no essential point; one must further draw out and reflect upon what is most essential within it and manifest it in practical measures, so that one's actions do not err on the side of pettiness and harshness, and may thereby benefit our people. If one acts thus, one's person is upright and one's words are trustworthy, one's righteousness is unified and one's actions are consistent—what could surpass this in the Way of being a minister! In general, the success or failure of governance is that upon which the security or peril, order or neglect of the state depend; ruler and minister, superior and inferior, truly cannot go a single day without planning for it. The Book of Documents (Shu) says: "In planning your governance, never fail to treat it as difficult; in abolishing and in initiating, go out and come in consulting the deliberations of your multitude, and when the words of the many agree, then think them through." Such was King Cheng of Zhou's admonition to Jun Chen on planning governance; is this not why King Cheng was able to carry on the illustrious achievements of the former kings and be an admirable ruler, and why Jun Chen was able to bring about harmonious and balanced rule and be a worthy minister!

Second Session

Discourse

"The Ruler of Men Is the Master of the People and Things of All under Heaven"

Wang Lu 王禄

論曰：以莫大之責付諸莫大之人，此大造之仁也。盖主天下之民物，責之大者也；處天下民物之上，人之大者也。以天下之人物，付之處天下民物之上之人君，豈徒然哉？盖將仁天下之民物，而代大造之仁，固天地之心，亦民物之心也。夫天地生物，厚於人，而尤厚於人君。其居之以地也，必於中國；其隆之以位也，必以大寶。是人君一身，中天地而立，天地之所賴也，天下之所宗也，民物之所仰而望也。豈有一民不歸掌握之中，一物不在範圍之内？其責何其大邪！責既大矣，責斯盡焉可也。彼為一家之主，則負一家之責也。苟子弟臧獲不得…
