Associate Examiner Senior Compiler Liu劉 comments: "The vital breath is full and the diction rich; it truly matches his work in the first session. Surely he is a scholar who has accumulated learning and awaits his moment!"
Examiner Librarian Jiang江 comments: "The principle is clear and the prose surges forth; reading it inspires respect and admiration."
Examiner Academician Wan萬 comments: "It brings out the meaning of the topic layer by layer; commendable."

The discourse reads: To entrust the greatest of responsibilities to the greatest of men—this is the benevolence of the Great Creator. For to be master over the people and things of All under Heaven is the greatest of responsibilities, and to occupy a position above the people and things of All under Heaven is to be the greatest of men. When the people and things of All under Heaven are entrusted to a ruler of men who occupies a position above them, how could this be in vain? Rather, it is so that he will treat the people and things of All under Heaven with benevolence and carry out the benevolence of the Great Creator on its behalf—which is indeed the mind of Heaven and Earth, and also the mind of the people and things. Now in giving life to things, Heaven and Earth are generous toward human beings, and especially generous toward the ruler of men. In placing him in a land, it is necessarily in the Central States; in exalting him with a position, it is necessarily with the Great Treasure [the throne]. Thus the ruler of men, in his single person, stands at the center between Heaven and Earth; he is the one upon whom Heaven and Earth rely, the one whom All under Heaven honor as their head, and the one toward whom the people and things look up in hope. How could there be a single person who does not come within his grasp, or a single thing that does not lie within his bounds? How great indeed is his responsibility! Since the responsibility is so great, it is only right that this responsibility be fulfilled. Take the master of a single household: he bears the responsibility for that household. If his younger kinsmen and bondservants do not attain…

title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
伏魚躍於二老來歸之日文王為民物之
主何如歸馬放牛於萬姓悅服之餘武王
為民物之主何若遠考列聖下俟將來人
君之責何如其盡哉彼飢者思飽田畜以
食之寒者思煖蠶桑以衣之匱者思以継
不橫征也勞者思以逸不妄役也自輦轂
之下至於海隅日出必使無一民之不被
吾仁然後可以為民之主否則譬諸滿堂
燕咲猶有向隅之泣謂之民之主未可也
===
山林之斧斤以時污池之數罟不入圍則
不合群則不掩自耳目之接至於窮山邃
谷必使無一物之不曁吾仁然後可以為
物之主否則譬諸萬彙皆生而一榦獨枯
則造化非全功謂之為物之主未可也民
而仁之斯不失之不足物而愛之斯不失
之有餘仁民愛物而民物之心始遂天地
之仁始得天下民物之主始無負矣設若
崇高享莫大之富貴威福操莫敵之勢拳

translation_en:
…crouched and fish leaped on the days when the two elders came in allegiance—what sort of lord of the people and creatures was King Wen? Horses were sent back and oxen turned loose after the myriad surnames gladly submitted—what sort of lord of the people and creatures was King Wu? Looking far back to the succession of sage-rulers and awaiting those to come in the future, how is the responsibility of a ruler to be fulfilled to the utmost?

Those who are hungry long to be full, so we promote farming and animal husbandry to feed them; those who are cold long to be warm, so we promote sericulture and mulberry cultivation to clothe them; those in want long for relief, so we do not impose tyrannical levies; those who toil long for rest, so we do not conscript them recklessly. From beneath the imperial chariot wheels out to the corners of the seas where the sun rises, one must ensure that there is not a single person who does not receive one's benevolence; only then can one be the lord of the people. Otherwise, it is like a hall full of banqueting and laughter where there is still someone weeping facing a corner—to call oneself the lord of the people is not yet permissible.

Axes and hatchets enter the mountain forests only according to the season, and fine-meshed nets do not enter the ponds and pools; in hunting, the encirclement is not closed completely, and herds are not ambushed wholesale. From what meets the eye and ear out to the remotest mountains and deepest valleys, one must ensure that there is not a single creature to which one's benevolence does not extend; only then can one be the lord of creatures. Otherwise, it is like all the myriad species coming to life while a single trunk alone withers—then the work of creation is not complete, and to call oneself the lord of creatures is not yet permissible.

By treating the people with benevolence, one does not err on the side of insufficiency; by cherishing creatures, one does not err on the side of excess. When one is benevolent to the people and cherishes creatures, only then are the hearts of the people and creatures satisfied, only then is the benevolence of Heaven and Earth attained, and only then does one not fail in being the lord of the people and creatures of the world. Suppose that, in exalted status, one enjoys matchless wealth and honor, and in doling out punishment and reward, one wields unrivaled power and authority [? 勢拳 for 勢權]…

…and gratifies his own desires and whims at the expense of the people and all living things—how could this be the mind of Heaven and Earth? And how could it be the mind of the people and all things? If it is not the mind of Heaven, Earth, the people, and all things, how can a ruler alone take his own selfish mind as the mind? This is clearly verified by the records of the past, and the supreme words of Master Zhen (Zhen Dexiu 真德秀) are well worth bearing in mind. In antiquity, Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, King Wen, and King Wu were the crowning exemplars of emperors and kings, far beyond reach; as for Gaozu and Emperor Wen of the Han, Taizong of the Tang, and Taizu of the Song, perhaps they came close! The cycle of Heaven's destiny revolves, and there is no going forth without a return; the role of lord over the people and all things must surely find its true home. Humbly reflecting upon our Dynasty, sage after sage has succeeded to the throne, the world turns toward their benevolence, and the people and all things rely on them for their very lives. Truly this is where Heaven's sincere assistance rests, and indeed where the intelligent and wise act as sovereigns. How fortunate are those born into this age! Your servant respectfully presents this discourse.

聞有以一而制萬者矣未聞以萬而制一
者也聞有以萬而統於一者矣未聞以一
而統於萬者也以一人之身而宰制乎民
物以民物之衆而倚命於一人此天地之
常經古今之大義於戲其盛矣哉夫君之
於民物以乾父坤母論之固同胞也固黨
與也君以一而兼主之豈無說乎武王曰
===

作元后元后作民父母此君之與民物得
乎天地者雖同而所以得乎天地者則異
以其異而制其同以其同而統於異此人
君所以混然雜於天下民物之中而卓然
立於天下民物之上固理也亦勢也盖嘗

斁矣有人君而五者以叙耳之於聲目之

I have heard of using the one to govern the myriad, yet never of using the myriad to govern the one; I have heard of the myriad being unified under the one, yet never of the one being subordinated under the myriad. For the person of a single man to rule and regulate the people and all things, and for the multitude of the people and all things to depend for their destiny upon a single man—this is the constant norm of Heaven and Earth and the great principle of past and present. Oh, how grand it is! Now, as for the ruler's relation to the people and all things, if we speak of it in terms of Qian as father and Kun as mother, they are indeed compatriots born of the same womb, and indeed comrades and fellows. That the ruler, as one, presides over both—how could this be without an explanation? King Wu said: "Heaven and Earth are the parent of all creatures; and of all creatures man is the most highly endowed. The sincerely intelligent becomes the great sovereign; and the great sovereign is the parent of the people." Thus, although what the ruler and the people and all things receive from Heaven and Earth is the same, that whereby they receive it from Heaven and Earth differs. By means of his difference he governs their sameness, and in their sameness they are unified under his difference. That the human ruler is thus blended amidst the people and creatures of the world, yet stands towering above the people and creatures of the world, is assuredly a matter of principle, and also of circumstance. 使天下不主於一人若網之無綱若裘之

挈之而不順也割之而不利也推之而不

況天下乎天下之不可無主盖如此則人

Those in danger desire security and those who toil desire ease; when there is a ruler of men to act as their master, those in danger are made secure and those who toil are given ease. That grain and millet in the fields and wilds are plowed and harvested according to the seasons, and that grasses and trees in the mountains and forests meet the axe and hatchet according to the seasons, is because there is a ruler of men to act as their master. Such is what it means for the empire to have a master. Therefore, the people of a single household must have a head; the ranks of the three armies must have a commander; a hamlet of ten households must have a steward. If this is true even of a single household, three armies, or ten households, how much more so of the empire? 君之於天下，有之則囂然者帖然以安，無之則寂然者鬨然以起。于以見一可以制萬，而萬不能制一也；萬有以統於一，而一不能統於萬也。

抑人君為天下民物之主，固然矣，而所以為之主者必有道焉。《易》曰：「君子體仁，足以長人。」《大學》曰：「為人君，止於仁。」仁也者，天地之心，民物之命。主民而非仁，則綏猷之責未副，時乂之功有歉；主物而非仁，則知之容有未盡，處之容有未當。一事而非仁，一事之失其主也；一息而非仁，一息之失其主也。苟徒以眇然之身而為之主，吾未見其能主也。善乎西山真氏之言曰：「人君為天下民物之主，痒痾疾痛，孰非同體？」故君道必主於仁，而為仁必極其至。然則世之主天下民物者，可不知所從事乎？欽惟先朝裁次格言，昭示君道，聖子神孫守為家法，愚敢為天下民物賀。謹論。
translation_en:
… ruler in relation to all under Heaven is such that when he is present, what is clamorous settles peacefully into tranquility; when he is absent, what is quiet rises up in tumult. From this we see that the one can govern the myriad, whereas the myriad cannot govern the one; the myriad have the means to be unified by the one, whereas the one cannot be unified by the myriad.

Moreover, that the ruler of men is the master of the people and creatures of all under Heaven is indeed so, yet that whereby he acts as their master must have its Way. The Classic of Changes (Yi) says: "The noble man, embodying benevolence, is sufficient to be a leader of men." The Great Learning (Daxue) says: "As a ruler of men, he abides in benevolence." Benevolence is the mind of Heaven and Earth, and the life of the people and creatures. If one acts as master of the people without benevolence, the responsibility of giving tranquility to their way of life is not fulfilled, and the achievement of bringing timely order falls short; if one acts as master of creatures without benevolence, one's understanding of them may not be exhaustive, and one's handling of them may not be fitting. If a single affair is not benevolent, that single affair has lost its master; if a single breath is not benevolent, that single breath has lost its master. If one merely relies on a puny physical body to act as their master, I have never seen that he is able to be a true master. Admirable indeed are the words of Mr. Zhen of Xishan (Zhen Dexiu 真德秀): "The ruler of men is the master of the people and creatures of all under Heaven; in their itching, sickness, illness, and pain, who among them is not of the same body with him?" Therefore, the Way of the ruler must take benevolence as its master, and the practice of benevolence must reach its utmost extreme. If this is so, how could those in the world who act as masters of the people and creatures of all under Heaven not know what they must devote themselves to? With reverence I reflect that a former reign edited and arranged these格言 (maxim-like words) to clearly manifest the Way of the ruler, and the sacred sons and divine grandsons have preserved them as family law; foolish as I am, I venture to offer congratulations on behalf of the people and creatures of all under Heaven. I respectfully present this discourse.

特達之深知？起自南宫，委之西事；固嘗受鉞，未成充國之功；將以息民，竟出魏絳之策。方國門之待罪，遽樞莞以承恩；懇避莫諧，貪榮是愧。兹盖伏遇〇〇〇〇，智出無為，仁而有勇；肇位四海，而機柄獨操；咸和萬民，而衡石不設。大以事小，恒施仁於小邦；安不忘危，每念戰為危事。用人如用藥，不遺馬勃牛溲；取士若取材，肯棄竹頭木屑？故兹迂拙，亦在甄收。臣敢不勉竭庸虚，上承知遇？感激難逢之會，奮勵無能之資；後樂先憂，期不負於素學；外攘内治，以無玷於清班。載看群策之兼收，坐致三邊之惕息。臣無任瞻天仰聖，激切屏營之至，謹奉表稱謝以聞。

第叄塲
translation_en:
…such exceptional and profound understanding? Recalled from the Southern Palace, I was entrusted with western frontier affairs; though I once received the battle-axe of command, I failed to achieve the merit of Zhao Chongguo; intending to give rest to the people, I ultimately resorted to the policy of Wei Jiang. Just as I was awaiting punishment at the gate of the capital, I suddenly received imperial favor at the Bureau of Military Affairs; my earnest pleas to decline were not granted, and I am ashamed of coveting such honor.

This is because I humbly encounter Your Majesty [〇〇〇〇], whose wisdom arises from non-action and who is benevolent yet courageous; establishing your rule over the Four Seas, you alone wield the lever of authority; bringing harmony to all the myriad people, you have no need to set up stone weights to measure documents. As a great state serving the small, you constantly extend benevolence toward minor states; in peace not forgetting danger, you are ever mindful that warfare is a perilous affair. Employing men as a physician uses medicine, you do not discard even puffball spores or cow's urine; selecting scholars as a builder selects timber, how would you cast aside bamboo ends or wood shavings? Thus even someone as pedantic and clumsy as I has been included in your discriminating selection.

How could Your Servant dare not strive to exhaust my mediocre and empty abilities to answer the recognition and favor received from above? Moved with gratitude at this rare opportunity, I rouse my incapable talents; rejoicing after the world rejoices and worrying before it worries, I hope not to betray what I have long studied; repelling external threats and ordering internal affairs, I seek to bring no blemish upon the pure ranks of officialdom. Looking ahead to the comprehensive adoption of all counsels, we shall effortlessly bring the three frontiers into respectful submission. Your Servant is overcome with the utmost emotion and trepidation in gazing up at Heaven and looking up to Your Sacred Majesty, and respectfully presents this memorial of gratitude for the Imperial hearing.

punctuated: 及而條陳之。《六經》，孔子刪述垂憲萬世者也。其間克盡夫斯道者，固未易毛舉；論其尤者，若堯之欽若，舜之勅天，敬孰愈焉？禹、皐在唐、虞，伊、旦在商、周，忠孰尚焉？舜之尊富饗保，武王、周公之繼志述事，孝孰加焉？大而可法者，豈外是哉！《四書》，孔門諸弟問答者也。其間有及夫斯道者，固未易縷陳；要其至，則戒懼之功、謹獨之力，皆敬也；勿欺之戒、堯舜之陳，皆忠也；無違之對、色難之警，皆孝也。切而易行者，寧越茲哉！洪惟我太祖高皇帝，萬幾之暇，修成《大誥》三編，于以頒示天下，于以曉告將來。語敬天也，則有不敬之條、報本之訓；語忠孝也，則有諭官之詞、明孝之章，無非闡明斯道也。又嘗致齋便殿，有感淵衷，爰命儒臣纂進《精誠錄》一書，以諭臣民，
translation_en: …touched upon, and set them forth point by point. The Six Classics are what Confucius edited and transmitted to leave as a model for ten thousand generations. Among them, those who were able to fulfill this Way completely are indeed not easy to enumerate in every detail; but to speak of the most outstanding examples: as for Yao's reverent accord with Heaven and Shun's cautious ordering under Heaven's mandate, what reverence could surpass theirs? With Yu and Gao Yao in the eras of Tang and Yu, and Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou (Dan) in the Shang and Zhou dynasties, what loyalty could be placed above theirs? With Shun's attaining supreme honor, wealth, ancestral offerings, and preservation of his posterity, and King Wu and the Duke of Zhou's carrying on their forebears' intentions and continuing their undertakings, what filial piety could exceed theirs? How could anything grand and worthy of emulation lie outside of these? The Four Books consist of questions and answers involving the disciples of Confucius's school. Among them, the passages that touch upon this Way are likewise not easy to recount thread by thread; but to sum up their highest essentials: the effort of being cautious and apprehensive and the exertion of watching over oneself when alone are both reverence; the admonition against deceiving one's ruler and the setting forth of the ways of Yao and Shun are both loyalty; the reply of "not disobeying" and the warning that "it is the countenance that is difficult" are both filial piety. How could anything pertinent and easy to practice go beyond this? I reflect upon how Our Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao (Taizu), in his leisure from a myriad of state affairs, compiled the three parts of the Grand Pronouncements (Dagao), thereby promulgating them to all under Heaven and instructing future generations. When speaking of revering Heaven, there are the articles on irreverence and the instructions on repaying one's origin; when speaking of loyalty and filial piety, there are the words admonishing officials and the chapters clarifying filial piety—none of which fails to elucidate this Way. Furthermore, while once observing a fast of purification in a side palace hall, being moved in the depths of his imperial heart, he thereupon commanded Confucian officials to compile and present the book Record of Utmost Sincerity (Jingcheng lu), so as to instruct his officials and people…

title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
以便
覽省或援引六經孔門之言或間及國語左
傳之說無非所以發明斯道也竊嘗讀誦
而仰窺我
高皇帝之聖心盖以為臣之於君親即天也忠
於君孝於親豈非敬天之實者乎君之祀
天地享宗廟臨兆民咸既厥心又非忠之
大者乎由是以觀則知敬天也忠君也孝
親也之三事者天下之達道上下所通行
===
而行之之要不外一心之精誠而已苟一
心精純而不雜誠實而無妄以之事天而
天心感以之事君而君心格以之事親而
親心悅由是三光明五行順百谷蕃身用
安榮家用平康禄位永保率於斯焉致否

之承順孝或徒養區區之口體亦何補邪

translation_en: …and so as to facilitate His own perusal and reflection. Whether citing the words of the Six Classics and the disciples of Confucius, or occasionally drawing upon the accounts in the Discourses of the States (Guoyu) and the Zuo Tradition (Zuozhuan), all of it was meant solely to elucidate this Way. I have humbly read and recited this work, and looking up to glimpse the sagely mind of our Emperor Gao, I believe He held that to a subject, one's ruler and parents are none other than Heaven itself. Are not loyalty to the ruler and filial piety toward one's parents the true substance of revering Heaven? And when the ruler sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, makes offerings at the ancestral temple, and governs the millions of people, exhausting his heart in all of these, is this not also the greatest form of loyalty? Viewed in this light, we know that revering Heaven, being loyal to the ruler, and being filial to one's parents—these three matters—are the universal Way of the world, practiced alike by those above and below; and the essential principle for putting them into practice lies in nothing other than the pure sincerity of the single mind. If the single mind is pure and unmixed, sincere and free of falsehood, then when one uses it to serve Heaven, the mind of Heaven is moved; when one uses it to serve the ruler, the mind of the ruler is reached; and when one uses it to serve one's parents, the minds of one's parents are delighted. From this, the three luminaries shine brightly, the Five Phases follow their proper order, the hundred grains flourish, one's person enjoys peace and honor, one's family enjoys tranquility and well-being, and one's emolument and rank are forever preserved—all of this is brought about hereby. Otherwise, if reverence consists merely in attending to petty ritual formalities, if loyalty consists merely in rendering obsequious compliance, and if filial piety consists merely in nourishing the physical body in a paltry way, of what avail is it? title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
昭代之明訓而究其要領欲致之於行求不
負天不負君不辱親自守以終身者也苟
弊弊於陳編汲汲於末務此非愚之素志
亦豈明執事之屬望於愚哉敷對至此不
知狂妄惟進而教之
第二問
華清
同考試官署員外郎趙批敷答問目節
節明白蓋博學之士歟
===
同考試官修撰劉批於諸說異同處剖析
明白可嘉
考試官洗馬江批所答切實必熟於本領者
考試官學士萬批辭簡而答亦明
對釋聖賢之書者有異說至朱子而始明
論聖賢之書者有異見得朱子而始定夫
朱子集諸儒之大成者也諸儒於四書聖
賢之言所論所見亦各有異焉非得朱子
而折衷之則厭常喜新穿鑿附會紛紜之

第二問
華清
同考試官署員外郎趙批：敷答問目，節節明白，蓋博學之士歟。

translation_en:
… the enlightened instructions of our illustrious dynasty, and investigated their essential principles, wishing to put them into practice and seeking not to fail Heaven, not to fail my sovereign, and not to disgrace my parents, maintaining myself thus throughout my life. Were I merely to toil away over stale texts and busy myself with trivial matters, this would not be my long-held aspiration, nor could it be what Your Excellency expects of me! Having set forth my reply to this point, I am unaware of my own rashness and presumption; I pray only that you admit me and instruct me.

Now, Master Zhu was the one who synthesized the great achievements of the various Confucians. Regarding the words of the sages and worthies in the Four Books, what the various Confucians discussed and perceived also differed from one another. Had it not been for Master Zhu weighing and reconciling them, then how could the tumultuous theories—tiring of the constant and delighting in novelty, forcing interpretations and making strained associations—…

title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
說將何由而明且定乎此子朱子之羽翼
四書有功於聖門也大矣學者烏容輕議
之哉粤自嬴秦既亡炎漢復興四書出於
孔壁之藏諸儒得於聞見之粗當時若馬
鄭服何之博學強記似能得論孟之奧旨
矣然或溺於卑近得其言而不得其意或
騖於高遠并其言而失之宜為朱子所不
取也自唐而宋若韓子蘇子為一時文章
魁傑似能究庸學之微意矣然一則語大
===
學而不言格物致知一則語中庸而不及
明善誠身宜為朱子所少也朱子謂論語
之要在於操存涵養如用力於一日三省
之餘致養於三月不違之後其用功孰切
焉謂孟子之要在於體驗擴充如即平旦
之氣以驗良心廣惻隱之發以保四海其
致力孰要焉大學首言明德新民一書之
綱領雖未嘗言敬然非敬則是二者何以
用力而止於至善此其始終不外乎敬也

綱領雖未嘗言敬然非敬則是二者何以
用力而止於至善此其始終不外乎敬也
punctuated: 說，將何由而明且定乎？此子朱子之羽翼《四書》，有功於聖門也大矣，學者烏容輕議之哉！粤自嬴秦既亡，炎漢復興，《四書》出於孔壁之藏，諸儒得於聞見之粗。當時若馬、鄭、服、何之博學強記，似能得《論》、《孟》之奧旨矣，然或溺於卑近，得其言而不得其意；或騖於高遠，并其言而失之，宜為朱子所不取也。自唐而宋，若韓子、蘇子為一時文章魁傑，似能究《庸》、《學》之微意矣，然一則語《大學》而不言格物致知，一則語《中庸》而不及明善誠身，宜為朱子所少也。朱子謂《論語》之要在於操存涵養，如用力於「一日三省」之餘，致養於「三月不違」之後，其用功孰切焉？謂《孟子》之要在於體驗擴充，如即「平旦之氣」以驗良心，廣「惻隱」之發以保四海，其致力孰要焉？《大學》首言明德、新民，一書之綱領雖未嘗言「敬」，然非敬，則是二者何以用力而止於至善？此其始終不外乎敬也。
translation_en: … [confused and conflicting] theories—how could they ever have been clarified and settled? In this way, Master Zhu [Zhu Xi 朱熹], in lending wings to the Four Books, rendered a great service to the school of the Sages; how could scholars lightly criticize him! Ever since the Ying Qin dynasty perished and the fiery Han revived, the Four Books emerged from where they had been hidden in the walls of Confucius's house, and the various Confucian scholars acquired only a rough understanding based on what they heard and saw. At that time, men of broad learning and retentive memory such as Ma [Ma Rong 馬融], Zheng [Zheng Xuan 鄭玄], Fu [Fu Qian 服虔], and He [He Yan 何晏 or He Xiu 何休] seemed capable of grasping the profound purport of the Analects (Lunyu) and the Mencius (Mengzi). Yet some sank into the shallow and near-at-hand, grasping the words while missing their meaning, whereas others galloped after the lofty and distant, losing even the words themselves; it was fitting that Master Zhu did not adopt their views. From the Tang to the Song, men like Master Han [Han Yu 韓愈] and Master Su [Su Shi 蘇軾 or Su Zhe 蘇轍] were the literary giants of their age and seemed capable of investigating the subtle meaning of the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong) and the Great Learning (Daxue). Yet the one discussed the Great Learning without speaking of the investigation of things and the extension of knowledge, while the other discussed the Doctrine of the Mean without touching upon understanding goodness and making the self sincere; it was fitting that Master Zhu held them in slight regard. Master Zhu held that the essential point of the Analects lies in preserving the mind and nurturing one's nature—such as exerting oneself in "examining oneself on three counts each day," and cultivating oneself to the point of "not departing from humaneness for three months"; what effort could be more earnest than this? He held that the essential point of the Mencius lies in personal realization and expansion—such as examining one's innate good mind through the "breath of the calm morning," and broadening the stirrings of "compassion" so as to protect all within the Four Seas; what endeavor could be more vital than this? The Great Learning begins by speaking of manifesting luminous virtue and renewing the people. Although the main outline of the entire book never explicitly mentions "reverence" (jing 敬), without reverence, how could one exert effort in these two things and come to rest in the highest good? Thus from beginning to end it goes nothing beyond reverence.

title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
中庸首言性道教一書之體要雖未嘗語
誠然是三者非誠則幾何而不淪於空虚
此其樞紐不出乎誠也程子言大學為入
德之門盖以指示初學也而鄒氏又謂六
經門戶自中庸入非取其慎獨一語乃君
子為己之要歟韓子言觀聖人之道自孟
子始盖以其能得所傳也而程子又謂才
高無據當學顏子非以其博約循序有地
之可據歟至於大學格物致知之傳朱子
===
取程子之意補之當矣而董氏乃謂錯簡
在經文中盖指知止能得一節而言辯則
辯矣要之當以朱子之言為定中庸尊德
性道問學之註朱子分存心致知釋之確
矣而饒氏輩乃以知行互有先後為說詳
則詳矣要之當以朱子之言為是大抵觀
聖賢之言不可不求其所言之理得其理
則諸儒之議論可得而定矣理同而言異
者不害其為同理苟不同言雖辯不足尚

punctuated: 《中庸》首言「性、道、教」，一書之體要雖未嘗語誠，然是三者非誠，則幾何而不淪於空虚？此其樞紐不出乎誠也。程子言《大學》為入德之門，盖以指示初學也；而鄒氏又謂「六經門戶自《中庸》入」，非取其「慎獨」一語乃君子為己之要歟？韓子言「觀聖人之道自孟子始」，盖以其能得所傳也；而程子又謂「才高無據，當學顏子」，非以其博約循序、有地之可據歟？至於《大學》「格物致知」之傳，朱子取程子之意補之，當矣；而董氏乃謂錯簡在經文中，盖指「知止能得」一節而言，辯則辯矣，要之當以朱子之言為定。《中庸》「尊德性、道問學」之註，朱子分存心、致知釋之，確矣；而饒氏輩乃以知行互有先後為說，詳則詳矣，要之當以朱子之言為是。大抵觀聖賢之言，不可不求其所言之理；得其理，則諸儒之議論可得而定矣。理同而言異者，不害其為同；理苟不同，言雖辯，不足尚…
translation_en: The Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong) opens by speaking of "human nature, the Way, and instruction"—the essential substance of the entire book. Although it does not yet explicitly speak of "sincerity" (cheng), without sincerity, how close would these three come to sinking into emptiness? Thus its pivot does not depart from sincerity. Master Cheng (Chengzi) said that the Great Learning (Daxue) is the gateway for entering into virtue, which was meant to point the way for beginners; yet Mr. Zou (Zou shi) also said that "the doorway to the Six Classics is entered through the Doctrine of the Mean"—was this not because he took its single phrase "being watchful over oneself when alone" (shendu) to be the essential point of the noble man's learning for self-improvement? Master Han (Han Yu) said that "observing the Way of the sages begins with Mencius," because Mencius succeeded in obtaining its transmission; yet Master Cheng also said that "for one whose talent is lofty but lacks a firm footing, one ought to learn from Master Yan (Yan Hui)"—was this not because his broadening through learning and restraining through ritual followed an orderly sequence and provided solid ground on which to stand? As for the commentary on "investigating things and extending knowledge" in the Great Learning, Master Zhu (Zhu Xi) drew upon the ideas of Master Cheng to supplement it, which was fitting; yet Mr. Dong (Dong槐, Dong Huai) maintained that the misplaced bamboo slips were actually within the classic text itself, referring to the passage on "knowing where to rest and being able to attain it." Ingenious as that argument is, in sum one ought to take Master Zhu's words as definitive. Regarding the commentary on "honoring the moral nature and following the path of inquiry and study" in the Doctrine of the Mean, Master Zhu explained them separately as preserving the mind and extending knowledge, which was exact; yet Mr. Rao (Rao Lu) and others advanced the theory that knowledge and action alternate in precedence. Detailed as that explanation is, in sum one ought to take Master Zhu's words as correct. Broadly speaking, when examining the words of the sages and worthies, one cannot fail to seek the principle of what they spoke; once one grasps their principle, the discussions of the various Confucian scholars can be settled. Where the principle is the same though the words differ, it does not harm their being the same; if the principle is not the same, even though the words are ingenious, they are not worth esteeming…

Now, having received your enlightened question, I venture to offer this in reply, though I do not know whether Your Excellency considers it so or not.

punctuated: 不自重以待用。故傅巖之築，必俟夢卜之求；莘野之耕，必俟再三之聘；渭水之釣，必俟後車之載。當時治道隆庬，風俗醇美，良有以夫。自是而後，人不逮古，俗漸下移。秦關燕璧之皇皇，高門懸簿之奔走，士始弗知以恬靜自重，人亦始以躁進為輕矣。方今聖天子在上，汲汲求賢，圖惟治理。養士於學校，羅士於科目。內而公卿大夫，簡拔於朝廷；外而藩臬守令，遴選於銓部。其或賢而沉匿下寮、隱處山林者，又有觀風之使薦焉。天子明此道於上，大臣明此道於下，所以養成恬靜之俗，而人才愈盛，治道愈隆，信不偶也。然而喬林千尋，豈無曲榦？嘉禾千頃，亦有稂莠。士之為士，豈盡能心賢君相之心哉？然欲嚴阻抑之法，則自重者無由而進，固不可也；隳法制之防，則僥倖者益啓其
translation_en:
…not maintain their self-respect while awaiting employment. Thus, the builder at Fuyan [Fu Yue 傅說] waited until he was sought through a dream and divination; the plowman in the fields of莘 (Shen) [Yi Yin 伊尹] waited until he was invited repeatedly with gifts; and the angler on the Wei River [Lü Shang 呂尚] waited until he was carried back in a rear carriage. At that time, the way of governance was grand and abundant, and customs were pure and admirable—truly for good reason! From then on, people did not measure up to antiquity, and customs gradually declined. With the anxious hurrying to the passes of Qin and for the jade discs of Yan, and the scurrying to hang one's name-tablet at high gates, scholars first ceased to know how to maintain self-respect through quiet contentment, and others likewise began to look down upon them for their impatient careerism.

At present, the Sacred Son of Heaven reigns above, eagerly seeking out the worthy and planning for good governance. He nurtures scholars in the schools and gathers them through the examination system. Within the capital, Dukes, Ministers, and Grand Masters are selected by the court; in the provinces, Provincial Administration Commissioners, Surveillance Commissioners, Prefects, and Magistrates are chosen by the Ministry of Personnel. As for those worthies who remain sunk in obscurity in minor posts or live in seclusion in the mountains and forests, there are also Commissioners Sent to Observe Local Customs to recommend them. The Son of Heaven makes this Way clear above, and the grand ministers make this Way clear below, thereby cultivating customs of quiet contentment; that talent becomes ever more flourishing and the way of governance ever more prosperous is truly no accident.

And yet, in a tall forest of a thousand *xun*, how could there be no crooked trunks? In a thousand *qing* of fine grain, there are also weeds. Among scholars, how could every single one take as his own mind the mind of a worthy ruler and his chief ministers? Yet if one wishes to tighten laws of obstruction and suppression, then those who maintain their self-respect will have no way to advance—which is certainly unacceptable. 心，又不可也。爲今之計，亦曰涵養之而已矣，作興之而已矣。涵養於未用之先，使皆明夫禮義廉恥之節；作興於已用之後，使皆崇夫端正純潔之行。若大臣之薦辟皆不通問訊之人，則雨及相門者卻矣；銓曹之選任皆十年不求磨勘之士，則考槃在澗者進矣。使恬退而得進者非終南之捷徑，又何患於人之趨其所不趨？使翕受而敷施者皆黎獻之共臣，又何患乎人主之無與理天下？轉移感動之機，端不待他求而有在矣。愚也荷教育之恩，服聖賢之訓，固不敢自棄於明時，亦未必盡同於流習。倘以爲可教而進之，則上不負天子，下不負所學，而圖効忠於萬一，將有日矣。

translation_en:
… ambitions, which is also unacceptable. As for a plan for the present, it is simply to nurture them and to inspire them, nothing more. By nurturing them before they are employed, cause them all to understand the moral integrity of propriety, righteousness, modesty, and a sense of shame; by inspiring them after they have been employed, cause them all to revere upright, pure, and unblemished conduct. If the recommendations and appointments made by great ministers are all of men who have never sent them greetings or inquiries, then those who brave the rain to call at the prime minister's gate will be turned away; if the selections and appointments made by the Ministry of Personnel are all of scholars who for ten years have not sought service evaluations for promotion, then those recluses who find joy in mountain streams will be advanced. If those who attain advancement through quiet modesty are not merely taking the "Zhongnan shortcut" to office, what worry could there be that men will rush after what they ought not to pursue? If those whose abilities are broadly received and put to work are all reverent subjects from among the eminent of the multitude, what worry could there be that the ruler has no one with whom to govern the realm? The pivotal mechanism for transforming and moving men's hearts truly lies right here and requires no search elsewhere. Ignorant as I am, having received the grace of imperial education and taken to heart the teachings of the sages and worthies, while I certainly dare not abandon myself in this enlightened age, neither do I necessarily conform completely to current customs. Should I be deemed teachable and advanced to office, then the day will come when above I shall not fail the Son of Heaven, below I shall not fail what I have learned, and I shall seek to render even one ten-thousandth of loyal service.

Question Four
Da Yi 達毅

…often know nothing at all about the proper measures for frontier defense. Only this essay cites antiquity to verify the present, with concrete proposals that can be put to practical use today. We record it here to await adoption by those who guard the frontiers.

Associate Examiner Examining Editor Wu [Wu] comments: This policy essay gathers historical precedents and weighs them to formulate what is feasible for the present day. It grasps the way in which the Central States control the western and northern barbarians, and must be the work of someone well-seasoned in the ways of the world. If someone is able to take this up and put it into practice, what difficulty would there be in achieving success!

Associate Examiner Senior Compiler Luo [Luo] comments: This policy question on military affairs was intended precisely to observe the practical learning of the candidates. It discusses the present while adducing antiquity, planning well without carelessness. Could an essay like this be by someone who has heard of frontier defense yet lacked prior study and discussion of it [?]? Seeing this in the final session, I could not help but leap with joy over it.

Examiner Mentor Jiang [Jiang] comments: It possesses both evidential grounding and insight; he is someone who, if employed, will certainly achieve practical results.

Examiner Academician Wan [Wan] comments: Citing antiquity to set forth the two strategies of offense and defense—this must be a man of high aspirations.

Response: The anxieties of meat-eaters are not what eaters of bean-leaves ought to deliberate upon; the anxieties of those who dwell in official mansions are not what those who dwell in humble alleys ought to manage. Now Your Excellency inquiries about military affairs of a mere scholar of chapter and verse—could it not be because you consider that beneath the potter's wheel of imperial transformation there might also be men living in obscurity who understand the affairs of the times, the likes of Zhuge Kongming [Zhuge Liang 諸葛亮] and Fan Zhongyan 范仲淹…

title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
戎而愚也非其人也雖然執事之念深矣
請借往事為執事籌之秦孝公之時河山
以東強國六淮泗之間小國十餘楚魏內
連戎狄外控然亦有勇於公戰怯於私鬭
之民如秦者乎亦有大小僇力務本重穡
之政如秦者乎民勇則足兵農重則足食
是殆未可以封域之大小為強弱也自元
朔取河南內地仁愿築朔方三城漢唐盛
時藉以制虜外阻大河為固內擅耕牧之
===
饒省內郡之轉輸减戍邊之吏士宋以靈
夏盡委之德明而河曲半擅於契丹中國
失控扼之險疆場無藩維之固是以夏之
服屬惟怵于遼而宋之奔命每疲於夏後
雖塞鴈門城大順然故境未復於漢唐驅
逐未還於河外殆難以五十步百步之遠
近為利害也自漢以前虜猶鈍拙土無剛
金國無良藝其後也拾遺戟於沉沙得漢
工於鮮卑勁弩強弓與漢爭巧控弦莫騎

工於解甲勁弩強弓與漢爭巧朝弦莫騎
punctuated: 戎？而愚也非其人也。雖然，執事之念深矣，請借往事為執事籌之。秦孝公之時，河山以東強國六，淮泗之間小國十餘，楚、魏內連，戎狄外控。然亦有勇於公戰、怯於私鬭之民如秦者乎？亦有大小僇力、務本重穡之政如秦者乎？民勇則足兵，農重則足食，是殆未可以封域之大小為強弱也。自元朔取河南內地，仁愿築朔方三城，漢、唐盛時藉以制虜，外阻大河為固，內擅耕牧之饒，省內郡之轉輸，减戍邊之吏士。宋以靈、夏盡委之德明，而河曲半擅於契丹，中國失控扼之險，疆場無藩維之固。是以夏之服屬惟怵于遼，而宋之奔命每疲於夏。後雖塞鴈門、城大順，然故境未復於漢、唐，驅逐未還於河外，殆難以五十步、百步之遠近為利害也。自漢以前，虜猶鈍拙，土無剛金，國無良藝。其後也，拾遺戟於沉沙，得漢工於鮮卑，勁弩強弓與漢爭巧，控弦莫騎…
translation_en:
… [? — likely a woodblock error for 哉], yet in my foolishness I am not that sort of person. Even so, Your Excellency's concern runs deep; permit me to draw upon past events to deliberate upon it for Your Excellency.

In the time of Duke Xiao of Qin 秦孝公, east of the Yellow River and the mountains there were six strong states, and between the Huai and Si rivers more than ten small states; Chu and Wei were linked within, while the Rong and Di barbarians held sway without. Yet did any of them have a populace brave in public warfare and timid in private brawls like that of Qin? Or a governance in which great and small joined their strength, attending to the fundamental occupation and prizing agriculture, like that of Qin? When the people are brave, there are sufficient troops; when agriculture is prized, there is sufficient food. Thus strength and weakness can hardly be measured by the size of a state's territory.

From the time the region south of the Yellow River was taken as interior territory during the Yuanshuo era [128–123 BCE], and Zhang Renyuan 張仁愿 built the three fortified cities of Shuofang, the Han and Tang in their heyday relied on these to control the northern caitiffs. Outside, they used the barrier of the Great River as a stronghold; inside, they commanded the abundance of farming and pasturage, sparing the interior commanderies the burden of transport and reducing the officers and men needed to garrison the frontier. The Song, however, abandoned all of Lingzhou and Xiazhou to Zhao Deming 趙德明, while half the Ordos bend of the Yellow River was dominated by the Khitan. The Central State lost the strategic passes by which to hold the enemy in check, and the borders lacked the security of a protective buffer. Consequently, Western Xia's submission was prompted solely by its fear of the Liao, while the Song was constantly exhausted rushing about at the mercy of Xia. Although later on the Song blockaded Yanmen Pass and fortified Dashun City, the old territories of the Han and Tang were not recovered, nor were the invaders driven back beyond the Yellow River; so one can hardly gauge advantage and harm by the difference between retreating fifty paces and retreating a hundred paces.

Before the Han, the caitiffs were still clumsy and crude; their land lacked hard metal, and their states lacked skilled craftsmanship. Later on, however, they picked up halberds left behind in the sunken sands and acquired Han artisans from the Xianbei; with stiff crossbows and strong bows they rivaled the Han in skill, while in drawing the bowstring as horsemen of the desert [? 莫騎 for 幕騎]…

title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
又虜所長當時所謂長技可復論乎夷虜
之性貪而無厭失利則奉頭鼠竄得利則
旦夕窺覦故定襄命帥突利入朝澶淵濟
師旃裘喪魄苟因之以為前却隨之以為
東西不致彼而致於彼則魏相所謂應兵
豈謂是乎故嘗探古今之變而極理勢之
論大都不出於戰守恩威而已彼来而敵
之謂戰彼攻而禦之謂守彼倔強而讋服
之之謂威彼順服而綏懷之之謂恩然不
===
戰則無以為守不威則無以為恩經城越
堡如蹈無人之境守將焉用狼子野心飼
之未必喜喜之未必馴恩將何施是故戰
必有可使之人守必有可據之地必有可
恃之實而後威可用必有可畏之勢而後
恩可施以言乎戰非聞鼙而踊鳴劍而嬉
不可使也非士飽而歌馬騰于槽不可使
也以言乎守我億萬之眾散之千里之邊
雖眾而寡彼數百之騎併力一堡之間雖

也以言乎守我億萬之衆散之千里之邊
雖衆而寡彼數百之騎併力一堡之間雖
punctuated: 又虜所長，當時所謂長技，可復論乎？夷虜之性，貪而無厭，失利則奉頭鼠竄，得利則旦夕窺覦。故定襄命帥，突利入朝；澶淵濟師，旃裘喪魄。苟因之以為前却，隨之以為東西，不致彼而致於彼，則魏相所謂應兵，豈謂是乎？故嘗探古今之變，而極理勢之論，大都不出於戰、守、恩、威而已。彼来而敵之之謂戰，彼攻而禦之之謂守，彼倔強而讋服之之謂威，彼順服而綏懷之之謂恩。然不戰則無以為守，不威則無以為恩。經城越堡，如蹈無人之境，守將焉用？狼子野心，飼之未必喜，喜之未必馴，恩將何施？是故戰必有可使之人，守必有可據之地，必有可恃之實而後威可用，必有可畏之勢而後恩可施。以言乎戰，非聞鼙而踊、鳴劍而嬉，不可使也；非士飽而歌、馬騰于槽，不可使也。以言乎守，我億萬之眾，散之千里之邊，雖眾而寡；彼數百之騎，併力一堡之間，雖…
translation_en: …are moreover what the nomads excel at. How can one still speak of what were considered our superior techniques in those earlier times? The nature of the barbarian nomads is greedy and insatiable: when they suffer a setback, they clutch their heads and scurry off like rats; when they gain an advantage, they spy and scheme morning and night. Thus, when a commander was appointed for the Dingxiang campaign, the Tuli Qaghan came to court to submit; when the imperial army crossed the river at Chanyuan, the felt-wearing nomads lost their nerve. If we merely advance or retreat in response to them, and move east or west following their lead—failing to compel them and instead being compelled by them—could this possibly be what Wei Xiang meant by "responsive troops"? Therefore, I have examined the changes from antiquity to the present and thoroughly analyzed the principles and circumstances: on the whole, they do not go beyond offensive warfare, defense, grace, and awe. When they come and we engage them, it is called warfare; when they attack and we resist them, it is called defense; when they are recalcitrant and we cow them into submission, it is called awe; when they submit and we pacify and cherish them, it is called grace. Yet without warfare there is no means to maintain defense, and without awe there is no means to bestow grace. If they pass by cities and cross over forts as though treading through an uninhabited land, of what use is defense? With the wild hearts of wolf cubs, feeding them will not necessarily please them, and pleasing them will not necessarily tame them—so how can grace be applied? Therefore, for warfare there must be men who can be deployed, and for defense there must be terrain that can be held; there must be reliable substance before awe can be exercised, and there must be a fearsome strategic advantage before grace can be bestowed. To speak of warfare: unless the men leap at the sound of the battle drums and delight in the ringing of their swords, they cannot be deployed; unless the soldiers are well-fed and singing, and the horses are prancing at their troughs, they cannot be deployed. To speak of defense: if our forces of hundreds of thousands are scattered along a frontier of a thousand li, though numerous they are few; if their several hundred horsemen concentrate their strength against a single fort, though…

title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
寡亦多故守得其要則力聚而強守失其
要則力分而弱受降據三面之固當千里
之蔽舍受降而衞東勝已失一面之險然
猶可說也東勝徑寧夏數百里列堡猶少
聚守猶專撤東勝以就延綏則舍數百里
之狭遮千餘里之衝無可說也以言乎威
則周宣不能無薄伐之師高宗不能無鬼
方之舉以言乎恩則米糒之賜必在於渭
橋鳴鐘之後磧口之賑必在於陰山露布
===
之餘大抵非霜雪無以為春非摧折無以
為長彼可略也吾之赤子寧不動念乎今
可忍也後之事會寧不預思乎推本而言
之則將領為重賞罰為先將領得人則據
形勝擇利便審攻守簡兵卒度張弛之計
審恩威之施無不得其當矣然將不以賞
罰御士則無以為將
朝廷不以賞罰馭將又何以成功斷斷乎其
不可易也欽惟

punctuated: 寡亦多。故守得其要，則力聚而強；守失其要，則力分而弱。受降據三面之固，當千里之蔽。舍受降而衞東勝，已失一面之險，然猶可說也；東勝徑寧夏數百里，列堡猶少，聚守猶專。撤東勝以就延綏，則舍數百里之狭，遮千餘里之衝，無可說也。以言乎威，則周宣不能無薄伐之師，高宗不能無鬼方之舉；以言乎恩，則米糒之賜，必在於渭橋鳴鐘之後，磧口之賑，必在於陰山露布之餘。大抵非霜雪無以為春，非摧折無以為長。彼可略也，吾之赤子寧不動念乎？今可忍也，後之事會寧不預思乎？推本而言之，則將領為重，賞罰為先。將領得人，則據形勝、擇利便、審攻守、簡兵卒、度張弛之計、審恩威之施，無不得其當矣。然將不以賞罰御士，則無以為將；朝廷不以賞罰馭將，又何以成功？斷斷乎其不可易也。欽惟
translation_en: …few, they are actually many. Therefore, if defense secures the strategic points, our strength is concentrated and strong; if defense loses the strategic points, our strength is divided and weak. The Shouxiang Cities occupied the security of three sides, serving as a screen for a thousand li. To abandon the Shouxiang Cities and defend Dongsheng was already to lose the natural barrier on one side, yet this could still be justified; the direct route from Dongsheng to Ningxia is only a few hundred li, so the forts arrayed there were still few, and concentrated defense was still focused. However, to withdraw from Dongsheng and fall back to Yansui is to abandon a narrow front of a few hundred li in order to block a strategic thoroughfare of over a thousand li—for this, no justification can be made. If we speak of awe-inspiring might, King Xuan of Zhou could not do without his expedition to punish the Xianyun, and King Gaozong of Shang could not do without his campaign against Guifang. If we speak of grace, the bestowal of grain and dried provisions must come after the striking of bells at the Wei Bridge, and relief at Qikou must follow the dispatch of victory proclamations from the Yin Mountains. In general, without frost and snow there is no way to bring about spring, and without breaking and pruning there is no way to foster growth. Even if those caitiffs can be overlooked, how could we not be moved to concern for our own infant subjects? Even if the present situation can be endured, how could we not think ahead to future contingencies? Speaking of the fundamental root of the matter, commanders are the most important, and rewards and punishments come first. When the right men are found as commanders, then occupying strategic terrain, choosing advantageous positions, judging between attack and defense, selecting and training soldiers, measuring plans for tension and relaxation, and deliberating the application of grace and might will all be handled properly. Yet if a commander does not govern his troops through rewards and punishments, he has no means to act as a commander; and if the Imperial Court does not control its commanders through rewards and punishments, how then can it achieve success? This is absolutely unalterable. Reverently I reflect that…

皇上宏天地之德一長育之心干羽同於虞舜

擇趙辛之畧蠢兹小虜不日于襄矣執事
無以為慮

馮廣
同考試官編修商批策以觀士子所蘊此

translation_en:
… His Majesty broadens the virtue of Heaven and Earth and unifies the mind of nourishing all things; his use of shield and feather in civil dance is the same as that of Yu Shun, and his punitive military prowess accords with that of the High Ancestor of Shang (Gaozong). The divine counsels of the imperial court already possess established strategies; to command the frontier, men as fine as Han Qi and Fan Zhongyan are employed, and to lead the troops, generals with the strategic acumen of Zhao Chongguo and Xin Qingji are chosen. These foolish petty caitiffs will be swept away before long; Your Excellency need not be concerned about them.

Fifth Question
Feng Guang 馮廣
Comment by Associate Examiner, Historiographer of the Hanlin Academy Shang: Policy essays serve to observe the learning a candidate has accumulated. This paper answers all five questions well, and on the topic of grain transport by canal (caoyun) in particular, it is able to cite past and present and weigh what is appropriate to the times. All of its proposals are concrete and practicable, which suffices to show a talent of real utility.
Comment by Associate Examiner, Senior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy Zhang: Among the papers in the examination hall on this policy question, some were imprecise regarding historical facts, while others were less than fitting in their proposed arrangements. What this paper replies flows abundantly and contains much worth adopting; the superiority of the candidate's learning and insight can be seen right here.
Comment by Associate Examiner, Expositor-in-waiting Peng: Current deliberations will likely have to follow this course.
Comment by Examiner, Librarian of the Supervisorate of Imperial Instruction Jiang: Answering each point as it is asked, without the slightest awkwardness or obstruction—how could anyone other than a scholar of true learning do so?
Comment by Examiner, Chancellor of the Hanlin Academy Wan: Able to recount past events and comprehend current affairs; it is worthy of selection.

title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
對論事必究利害之原興事必度重輕之
計莫不有利害也而利害之末流君子所
不恤莫不有重輕也而重輕之大分君子
不之苟此籌國之遠猷達時之大義若夫
駭紛紜於目睫眩岐路於東西惡足以語
此哉嗟夫漕運之倚賴於國家也尚矣利
害之關繫於斯民也不細矣得其人則國
足而民安不得其人則國匱而民病未有
能易之者也嘗博觀前載頗悉顛委西京
===
===
之初海陵貯東南之粟江淮固封植之私
是以關中調度悉仰山東然始也僅數十
萬而已及武帝以後益而為百萬餘石又
益而為四百萬石且至六百萬石焉唐室
初造外漕甚約自河北入藩鎮之圖山東
有疆場之擾京師之用悉仰江淮故天寶
每歲二百五十萬廣德歲轉亦不下百一
十萬焉宋漕法分為四路東南之粟自
汴河而至自黃河而入陳蔡之粟自
汴河而至陝西之粟自黃河而入陳蔡之

汴河而至陝西之粟自黃河而入陳蔡之
punctuated: 對：論事必究利害之原，興事必度重輕之計。莫不有利害也，而利害之末流，君子所不恤；莫不有重輕也，而重輕之大分，君子不之苟。此籌國之遠猷，達時之大義。若夫駭紛紜於目睫，眩岐路於東西，惡足以語此哉！嗟夫！漕運之倚賴於國家也尚矣，利害之關繫於斯民也不細矣。得其人則國足而民安，不得其人則國匱而民病，未有能易之者也。嘗博觀前載，頗悉顛委。西京之初，海陵貯東南之粟，江淮固封植之私，是以關中調度，悉仰山東。然始也僅數十萬而已，及武帝以後，益而為百萬餘石，又益而為四百萬石，且至六百萬石焉。唐室初造，外漕甚約。自河北入藩鎮之圖，山東有疆場之擾，京師之用，悉仰江淮。故天寶每歲二百五十萬，廣德歲轉亦不下百一十萬焉。宋漕法分為四路：東南之粟自汴河而至，自黃河而入，陳、蔡之粟自汴河而至，陝西之粟自黃河而入，陳、蔡之
translation_en:
Reply: In discussing affairs, one must investigate the source of advantages and disadvantages; in undertaking enterprises, one must weigh the calculation of what is weighty and what is light. There is nothing that does not have advantages and disadvantages, yet the minor consequences of advantages and disadvantages are what the gentleman does not trouble over; there is nothing that does not have what is weighty and what is light, yet the great distinction between the weighty and the light is what the gentleman does not treat casually. This is the far-reaching counsel for planning the state, and the great principle for understanding the times. As for those who are startled by confusion right before their eyelashes or dazzled by diverging roads to the east and west, how could they be worthy of discussing this! Alas! The state's reliance upon grain transport by water (caoyun) is of long standing, and its bearing on the welfare of the people is by no means trivial. When the right men are obtained, the state is well-supplied and the people are at peace; when the right men are not obtained, the state is depleted and the people suffer—there has never been anyone able to alter this principle.

I have extensively examined the records of former times and know the full story quite thoroughly. At the beginning of the Western Han [Western Capital], Hailing stored the grain of the southeast, and the Jiang-Huai region was held as the private domain of enfeoffed princes; therefore, the provisioning of Guanzhong relied entirely upon Shandong [the region east of the passes]. Yet in the beginning it was merely several hundred thousand piculs (shi). By the time of Emperor Wu and afterward, it increased to over one million piculs, then increased further to four million piculs, and even reached six million piculs. When the Tang house was first founded, grain transport from the provinces was very modest. Once Hebei fell into the hands of the regional military governors (fanzhen) and Shandong suffered border disturbances, the needs of the capital relied entirely upon the Jiang-Huai region. Thus in the Tianbao era (742–756) the annual amount was 2,500,000 piculs, and in the Guangde era (763–764) the annual transport was still no less than 1,100,000 piculs. Under the Song, the grain transport system was divided into four routes: the grain of the southeast arrived by way of the Bian River, [? entered by way of the Yellow River, the grain of Chen and Cai] arrived by way of the Bian River, the grain of Shaanxi entered by way of the Yellow River, the grain of Chen and Cai…

title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
粟自惠民河通之京師之粟自廣濟河通
之率計江淮之入十倍三路之數此其大
較也究而論之則汴宋之千艘西上不若
府制之寓兵於農弘羊以剥民為進身之
計不若劉晏以養民為足國之本他如疏
引雜斂之規轉般直達之法雖有可言無
足論也我
太祖高皇帝定鼎金陵都四方之會
太宗文皇帝肇建京師據天下之勝自海舟罷
===
直沽之運常盈列淮浦之倉軍國經費全
仰東南轉兌用坐食之兵督運授分閫之
寄區畫精詳講求周悉民不告勞國用以
足六十年于茲
太宗之貽謀恭襄之偉績何其盛哉夫自真揚
以至通州水行四十餘驛閘壩相次亭堠
相望此
先朝宏遠之謨也自通州距都城陸輓僅五
十里故閒置官廢渠設卒此

translation_en:
… grain was conveyed via the Huimin River, and the grain of the京东 [?京師] region was conveyed via the Guangji River. Broadly calculated, the revenue coming in from the Jiang-Huai region was ten times the amount of the other three routes combined. This is the general outline. If we examine and discuss the matter thoroughly, the thousand barges of the Bianliang Song sailing westward were inferior to the garrison militia system (fuzhi), which embedded soldiers among the peasantry; and Sang Hongyang’s scheme of exploiting the people to advance his own career was inferior to Liu Yan’s principle of nourishing the people as the foundation for enriching the state. As for other measures—such as the regulations for dredging channels and miscellaneous levies, or the methods of relay shipping (zhuanban) and direct delivery (zhida)—although there are things that could be said of them, they are not worth discussing.

Our Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao (Taizu), established the imperial tripod at Jinling, making his capital at the crossroads of the four quarters; our Grand Ancestor, Emperor Wen (Taizong), founded the northern capital, occupying the most strategic site in the realm. Ever since sea vessels ceased the transport to Zhigu and the Changying Granaries were arrayed along the banks of the Huai, the regular expenditures of the military and the state have relied entirely upon the southeast. For transfer and commutation (zhuandui), idle troops who would otherwise merely sit and consume rations are employed; for supervising the transport, commanders entrusted with regional military authority are appointed. The planning has been precise and detailed, and the deliberations thorough and comprehensive. The common people do not complain of toil, and the state’s fiscal needs are thereby met. For sixty years until now, how magnificent have been the far-sighted plans bequeathed by Taizong and the great achievements of Gongxiang [Chen Xuan, Marquess Gongxiang]! Now, from Zhenzhou and Yangzhou all the way to Tongzhou, the water route spans more than forty postal relay stations, with locks and dams following one after another and watchtowers and mile-mounds in sight of each other—this was the grand and far-reaching plan of the former reigns. From Tongzhou to the capital city, overland haulage is a mere fifty li, so officials are still appointed to the old locks [reading 閒 as 閘] and soldiers stationed along the disused canal—this is …

title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
先朝未究之志也迩来漕法漸隳軍民俱困
僦車之費罷敝莫勝
皇上因群臣之議
特詔修復蓋欲承
文皇帝圖就之志按郭太史疏鑿之遺興軍民
悠久之利而衆論紛然莫之適主竊以為
原漕事之利害則不在於五十里之車牛
而在於二十萬之將領計役事之重輕則
不患其不能必有所為而患其不能大有
===
所為何則以漕事論之則出辦煩於科率
派搭擾於差數羡費盡於般剥贏財恣於
飲食舟未至而其人已病矣况加以陸輓
之困邪語云強弩之末不能穿魯縞况非
魯縞乎又曰行百里者半九十况非九十
乎使恭襄之制節尚存舟師之饒裕自若
雖僦車可也雖重費可也以役事而論之
則漢穿引渭之渠唐避三門之險開寶中
創鄲濟五丈之河永樂中通安民百里之

translation_en:
… was the unfulfilled ambition of the former reigns. In recent times, the regulations for grain transport have gradually fallen into decay, and both soldiers and civilians are distressed. Exhausted and worn out, they cannot bear the expense of hiring carts. In response to the deliberations of the court officials, His Majesty issued a special decree to restore the canal, wishing thereby to carry forward the Cultured Emperor's [Yongle's] ambition to bring the plan to completion, to follow the traces of the dredging and excavation left by Grand Astrologer Guo [Guo Shoujing 郭守敬], and to establish a lasting benefit for both the military and the people. Yet public opinion is in a tumult, with no agreement on what course to follow.

I humbly submit that if we trace the advantages and disadvantages of the grain transport, the crux lies not in the carts and oxen over those fifty li, but in the commanders and officers leading the two hundred thousand troops; and if we weigh the relative gravity of the construction project, the worry is not whether we can manage to accomplish something, but whether we can accomplish it on a grand scale. Why is this so?

Speaking in terms of the grain transport itself: procuring supplies is made burdensome by arbitrary levies; apportioning cargoes is thrown into confusion by irregular quotas; surplus allowances are exhausted by transshipment and lighterage; and remaining funds are squandered on food and drink. Before the boats have even arrived, the men are already worn out—how much worse when the hardship of overland hauling is added to it! As the saying goes, "An arrow at the end of its flight from a strong crossbow cannot pierce the thin silk of Lu"—how much less when what faces it is tougher than the silk of Lu! Another saying goes, "For one traveling a hundred li, ninety li is only halfway"—how much more so when the journey is far beyond ninety li! If the regulations and economies instituted by Gongxiang [Chen Xuan 陳瑄] still remained, and the boatmen enjoyed their former abundance and ease, then even hiring carts would be bearable, and even heavy expenses would be acceptable.

Speaking in terms of the construction project: the Han excavated the canal drawing water from the Wei River; the Tang bypassed the perils of the Sanmen Gorges; during the Kaibao era [968–976], the Wuzhang Canal was opened between Yun and Ji; and during the Yongle era [1403–1424], a hundred li through Anmin …

title: 成化八年會試錄
text:
山犯難而動真有成績夫以六軍萬姓之
力為六軍萬姓之計興五十里踰丈之役何
嫌何疑而有前却况京城至通州地形高
下纔五十尺以五十里之遠近攤五十尺
之高低何所不可苟有任事之人有見逺
之畫浚甕山泊以蓄西山諸水引神山泉
以合下流之歸迂廻以順其地形因時以
謹其濬治一勞而永佚暫費而大蠲未有
不可也若小小經營草草疏濬苟且滅裂
===

之策無大損益徒或擾煩而以力之屈乗
歳之虛雖不興可也雖付之莫可如何可
也一得之見或有中焉則今日之幸

translation_en:
… Mountain; braving difficulties to take action, they truly achieved real results. Now, using the strength of the Six Armies and the myriad people to make plans for the Six Armies and the myriad people, and undertaking a labor project fifty li in length and over a zhang in depth—what cause is there for suspicion or doubt that one should hesitate to go forward? Moreover, from the capital city to Tongzhou, the difference in elevation of the terrain is barely fifty chi. Spreading a fifty-chi difference in height over a distance of fifty li, what is impossible about that? If there are men willing to shoulder responsibility and possessed of far-sighted plans—dredging Wengshan Lake to store the various waters of the Western Hills, channeling the Shenshan Spring to join the convergence of the lower reaches, making the course wind so as to follow the lay of the land, and taking advantage of the proper seasons to attend carefully to its dredging and maintenance—then through one effort there will be eternal ease, and through temporary expenditure there will be a great remission of burdens; there is nothing in this that cannot be done.

If, however, one engages in petty management and perfunctory dredging, acting in a makeshift and slipshod manner and merely following old routines, so that boats do not enjoy the benefit of unimpeded passage and the locks and dams still rely on the method of transshipment, then there will be no great gain or loss, and it will only cause disturbance and trouble. When labor is exhausted and the harvest of the year is poor, even not undertaking the project at all is permissible, and even resigning oneself to there being nothing that can be done about it is permissible. If this humble opinion happens to hit the mark, it will be the good fortune of the present day.

Postface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

In the spring of the renchen year of the Chenghua era [1472], scholars from throughout the realm gathered in the capital for the Metropolitan Examination. When the Ministry of Rites petitioned for the appointment of Examiners, His Majesty the Emperor decreed that Your Servants [Wan] An and [Jiang] Chaozong go forth to preside over the literary evaluations. Reverently receiving His benevolent intent, we dared not be negligent or remiss. Together with the various officiating functionaries, we exhorted one another and exhausted our minds in the earnest pursuit of true talent. It was like panning for gold in the sand or carving jade from the uncut stone—not stopping until the gold is obtained and the jade is revealed. Once we found the right men, we recorded their names together with the finest of their essays to present to His Majesty.
